lessons.title: Further integration techniques
lessons.summary: Choose a substitution or a standard inverse-function form.
lessons.objective: Evaluate integrals with quadratic roots and hyperbolic substitutions, including endpoint limits.
lessons.before: Review substitution, integration by parts and partial fractions from Pure Mathematics. Complete inverse hyperbolic functions and the chain rule. Mean values and volumes used in some written problems are prerequisite applications, not new Further Mathematics requirements.
lessons.ideas:
Recognise the expression under the root

Complete the square before choosing a substitution. For a positive constant a, the three common patterns are \(a^{2}\)−\(u^{2}\), \(a^{2}\)+\(u^{2}\) and \(u^{2}\)−\(a^{2}\). Real domains and the positive square root determine the useful branch.

\[\begin{gathered}\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{a^2-u^2}}=\sin^{-1}\frac ua+C\\\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{a^2+u^2}}=\sinh^{-1}\frac ua+C\\\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2-a^2}}=\cosh^{-1}\frac ua+C\quad(u>a)\end{gathered}\]

For u<−a the last expression needs a different branch or a logarithmic absolute-value form. A standard form in u still requires the factor from du/dx.

Make the radical manageable

Use u=a sin v for a circular root and u=a sinh v for a sum of squares. For \(u^{2}\)−\(a^{2}\) on u≥a, use u=a cosh v with v≥0. Then sqrt(sin\(h^{2}\)v)=sinh v on that branch. Transform both endpoints together with the differential.

Improper does not automatically mean divergent

If the integrand is unbounded at an endpoint, first integrate over a shorter interval and then take its one-sided limit. A finite primitive limit can still give a finite integral. Do not substitute an undefined endpoint into the original integrand.

Choose what the quantity measures

\[\begin{gathered}\bar f=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\\V=\pi\int_a^b y^2\,dx\end{gathered}\]

These prerequisite formulae are different from arc length and curved surface area. Check the variable with respect to which an average is requested.
lessons.method:
1. Complete the square and identify the real interval.
  2. Choose a direct inverse form or write a reversible substitution.
  3. Transform the differential and both limits.
  4. Integrate, applying a one-sided limit at an improper endpoint.
  5. Differentiate the primitive to check the scale and branch.
mistakes: The derivative of an inner linear expression contributes a scale factor.
The principal square root is non-negative.
Change limits only when the integration variable changes.
An infinite endpoint value of the integrand does not prove divergence.
A mean, a volume and a surface area use different integrands.

examples.title: 1 · Complete the square first
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_1^3(16-(x-1)^2)^{-1/2}\,dx\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}u=x-1,\qquad0\le u\le2\\\int_0^2\frac{du}{\sqrt{16-u^2}}\\=\left[\sin^{-1}\frac u4\right]_0^2=\frac\pi6\end{gathered}\]

The root is positive throughout the interval. No extra factor appears because du=dx.

examples.title: 2 · A linear scale in a hyperbolic inverse
examples.question: Find \(\int(9+4x^2)^{-1/2}\,dx\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}u=2x,\qquad dx=\frac12du\\\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9+4x^2}}\\=\frac12\sinh^{-1}(\frac{2x}{3})+C\end{gathered}\]

The factor 1/2 comes from the differential. Differentiate the result to check it.

examples.title: 3 · A convergent improper endpoint
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_2^{5/2}(x^2-4)^{-1/2}\,dx\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=2\cosh u,\qquad00)\\\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{2+\varepsilon}^{5/2}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-4}}=\ln2\end{gathered}\]

At the upper limit cosh u=5/4, so u=ln2. At the lower limit u tends to zero. The singularity is integrable.

examples.title: 4 · A hyperbolic substitution for a root
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{3/2}\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=2\sinh u,\quad0\le u\le\ln2\\\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx=4\cosh^2u\,du\\\int4\cosh^2u\,du=2u+\sinh2u\\\int_0^{3/2}\sqrt{x^2+4}\,dx\\=2\ln2+\frac{15}{8}\end{gathered}\]

Use cos\(h^{2}\)u=(1+cosh2u)/2 and retain the transformed limits.

lessons.title: Algebraic and exponential reduction formulae
lessons.summary: Derive a recurrence, then start from the correct base case.
lessons.objective: Establish endpoint-aware recurrences and use them without accumulating rounding errors.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Retain exact values until the final numerical step.

Some written extensions use induction to establish a coefficient formula or a bound. Review proof by induction before those parts.
lessons.ideas:
A recurrence is an identity between integrals

For a family Iₙ, choose an integration-by-parts step or differentiate a suitable product. Rewrite its derivative using the family integrands, integrate over exactly the given interval, and evaluate the boundary term. State the indices for which every term is defined.

\[\begin{gathered}H_n^{\prime}(x)=A_n f_n(x)+B_n f_{n-1}(x)\\A_nI_n+B_nI_{n-1}=H_n(b)-H_n(a)\end{gathered}\]

The boundary term may depend on n

Do not erase a lower endpoint merely because one example made it zero. A factor \(x^{n}\) vanishes at zero when n>0, but not when n=0. This is one reason the recurrence can have a stricter index range than the integral definition.

Match the starting index to the step

A step of one uses I₀ or I₁ as appropriate; a step of two splits the family into odd and even chains. Compute each needed base integral directly. For an indefinite family include an arbitrary constant in the final antiderivative.

Carry evidence into later conclusions

For an induction claim, state the base case, assume the result at the previous relevant index, and insert it into the proved recurrence. A numerical initial value has an error: a linear recurrence propagates that error by the absolute value of its coefficient. Round only once at the end.
lessons.method:
1. Write the family and its valid indices.
  2. Differentiate a useful product or integrate by parts.
  3. Express the result using family members and evaluate both boundaries.
  4. Find the necessary base integral and follow the correct parity chain.
  5. Keep exact values and justify any bound or propagated error.
mistakes: A recurrence without its boundary term is generally false.
An n=0 case can differ from the n≥1 cases.
A two-step recurrence needs a base of the same parity.
An induction proof requires both a base and a general step.
Do not round each intermediate recurrence value.

examples.title: 1 · A logarithmic family
examples.question: Let \(I_n=\int_1^{e^3}(\ln x)^n\,dx\). Derive a recurrence and find I₂.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}I_n=3^ne^3-nI_{n-1}\quad(n\ge1)\\I_0=e^3-1,\qquad I_1=2e^3+1\\I_2=5e^3-2\end{gathered}\]

Take u=(ln x)ⁿ and dv=dx. The lower endpoint contribution is zero only for n≥1.

examples.title: 2 · A rational-root family
examples.question: For \(J_n=\int_0^1(1+x^2)^{-n}\,dx\), derive a recurrence and evaluate J₂.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac d{dx}\{x(1+x^2)^{-n}\}\\=(1-2n)(1+x^2)^{-n}\\\quad+2n(1+x^2)^{-n-1}\\(1-2n)J_n+2nJ_{n+1}=2^{-n}\\J_1=\frac\pi4,\qquad J_2=\frac14+\frac\pi8\end{gathered}\]

The recurrence holds for n≥1. Solve it for Jₙ₊₁ to move towards the requested integral.

examples.title: 3 · A positive integral gives an exponential bound
examples.question: Let \(K_n=\int_0^1(1-x)^ne^x\,dx\). Find K₂ and use 0<K₂<1/2 to bound e.
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}K_n-nK_{n-1}=-1\quad(n\ge1)\\K_0=e-1,\quad K_1=e-2\\K_2=2e-5,\qquad\frac52On 0<x<1, (1−x)eˣ<1 because its derivative is −xeˣ<0. Therefore 0<(1−x)²eˣ<1−x. Integrate to obtain the strict bound before rearranging.

examples.title: 4 · Propagating an input error
examples.question: A proved recurrence gives \(J_2=\frac16+\frac12J_1\) and \(J_3=\frac1{36}+\frac34J_2\). If the supplied J₁ has error at most 10⁻⁶, bound the induced error in J₃.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}J_3=\frac{11}{72}+\frac38J_1\\|\Delta J_3|\le\frac38\times10^{-6}\end{gathered}\]

The constants contribute no input error. Multiply the two recurrence coefficients, then take the absolute value. This excludes any separate final-output rounding.

lessons.title: Trigonometric and hyperbolic reductions
lessons.summary: Use identities to turn derivatives into the integral family.
lessons.objective: Derive and apply reductions involving trigonometric and hyperbolic powers.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Retain exact values until the final numerical step.
lessons.ideas:
Choose a product that lowers a power

For powers of sine, a product si\(n^{n-1}\)x cos x produces both si\(n^{n}\)x and si\(n^{n-2}\)x after differentiation and use of co\(s^{2}\)x=1−si\(n^{2}\)x. State n≥2 and evaluate the endpoints. The same idea works with hyperbolic identities, but their signs differ.

\[\begin{gathered}\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x\\\cosh^2x=1+\sinh^2x\\\operatorname{sech}^2x=1-\tanh^2x\end{gathered}\]

A frequency is part of the differential

For sin(kx), derivatives and primitives introduce k and 1/k. A substitution u=kx changes the limits and gives dx=du/k. Keep these scale factors when a recurrence is used in a volume or another integral application.

Sometimes subtract before integrating

Neighbouring integrands can have a much simpler difference or sum. For example, cancelling a factor with 1−si\(n^{2}\)x can leave a direct substitution. This can give a first-step recurrence without integration by parts.

Choose the correct chain and domain

An even power target and an odd power target may have different base integrals. Secant and cotangent families must avoid poles on the integration interval, or be handled as improper integrals with justified convergence. Do not use a recurrence to assign a finite number to a divergent integral.
lessons.method:
1. Differentiate the suggested product or combine neighbouring integrands.
  2. Apply the matching trigonometric or hyperbolic identity.
  3. Keep the frequency factors and endpoint values.
  4. State valid indices and find the required odd or even base.
  5. Evaluate exactly, checking positivity when the integrand is non-negative.
mistakes: Circular and hyperbolic identities have different signs.
Do not lose the frequency in sin(kx) or cosh(kx).
A recurrence stepping by two preserves parity.
Check for poles before evaluating a definite integral.
A non-negative integrand cannot have a negative integral.

examples.title: 1 · A sine-power reduction
examples.question: Let \(I_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx\). Derive the reduction and find I₄.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac d{dx}(\sin^{n-1}x\cos x)\\=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x-n\sin^nx\\nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}\quad(n\ge2)\\I_0=\frac\pi2,\quad I_2=\frac\pi4,\quad I_4=\frac{3\pi}{16}\end{gathered}\]

Both product endpoints vanish for n≥2. The even chain starts from I₀.

examples.title: 2 · A cosh family with a non-zero boundary
examples.question: Let \(C_n=\int_0^{\ln3}\cosh^nx\,dx\). Derive a recurrence and find C₂.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}nC_n-(n-1)C_{n-2}\\=\frac43\left(\frac53\right)^{n-1}\quad(n\ge2)\\C_0=\ln3,\qquad C_2=\frac{10}{9}+\frac12\ln3\end{gathered}\]

Differentiate sinh x cos\(h^{n-1}\)x and replace sin\(h^{2}\)x by cos\(h^{2}\)x−1. The upper endpoint uses sinh(ln3)=4/3 and cosh(ln3)=5/3.

examples.title: 3 · Subtract neighbouring integrands
examples.question: Let \(A_n=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^{2n}x/\cos x\,dx\). Derive Aₙ−Aₙ₊₁ and find A₁.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}A_n-A_{n+1}=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^{2n}x\cos x\,dx\\=\frac{2^{-(2n+1)}}{2n+1}\quad(n\ge0)\\A_0=\frac12\ln3,\qquad A_1=\frac12\ln3-\frac12\end{gathered}\]

The subtraction supplies co\(s^{2}\)x in the numerator. Then u=sin x gives a power integral.

examples.title: 4 · A scaled prerequisite volume
examples.question: The region under \(y=3\sin^2(2x)\) for \(0\le x\le\pi/4\) is rotated about the x-axis. Find its volume.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}V=9\pi\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^4(2x)\,dx\\=\frac{9\pi}{2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4u\,du\\=\frac{27\pi^2}{32}\end{gathered}\]

The square on y produces sine to the fourth power; u=2x contributes 1/2. Use the previously proved even sine recurrence.

lessons.title: Arc length in Cartesian, parametric and polar form
lessons.summary: Integrate speed, keeping its non-negative branch.
lessons.objective: Set up and evaluate arc lengths without assuming monotone horizontal motion.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Retain exact values until the final numerical step.

Review parametric derivatives and polar coordinates. A polar arc-length application uses the formula derived here.
lessons.ideas:
A small displacement has a length

\[\begin{gathered}ds=\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}\\L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}\,dx\\L=\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{(X^{\prime})^2+(Y^{\prime})^2}\,dt\end{gathered}\]

Use the first form for a single-valued y(x) over increasing x. The parametric speed remains non-negative even if X′ changes sign or is zero. The integral measures the path traversed; check whether the chosen parameter interval retraces a curve.

Perfect squares still need a sign check

Algebra may give spee\(d^{2}\)=g(t)². Then speed=|g(t)|. Remove the absolute value only after examining g on the whole interval, and split where necessary. An isolated zero speed does not by itself prevent a finite length.

Polar length follows from Cartesian coordinates

Differentiate X=r cos θ and Y=r sin θ. The cross terms cancel when the derivative squares are added.

\[\begin{gathered}\left(\frac{ds}{d\theta}\right)^2=r^2+\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2\\L=\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{r^2+(r^{\prime})^2}\,d\theta\end{gathered}\]

Length is different from area

A polar area uses half the integral of \(r^{2}\); it does not give a length. Keep the original endpoints and symmetry factors explicit. Units for a length are linear units.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the representation and the exact parameter interval.
  2. Differentiate each coordinate before squaring.
  3. Simplify the speed squared, then check the square-root sign.
  4. Integrate the non-negative speed over one traversal.
  5. Check endpoints, symmetry factors and linear units.
mistakes: For parametric length use speed, not dy/dx alone.
The square root of a square is an absolute value.
Negative horizontal velocity does not give negative length.
A polar area formula is not an arc-length formula.
Check that a parameter interval does not retrace the same arc.

examples.title: 1 · A Cartesian power curve
examples.question: Find the length of \(y=\frac23x^{3/2}\) from x=0 to x=3.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y^{\prime}=\sqrt x,\qquad\frac{ds}{dx}=\sqrt{1+x}\\L=\left[\frac23(1+x)^{3/2}\right]_0^3=\frac{14}{3}\end{gathered}\]

The lower endpoint is included by continuity of the speed.

examples.title: 2 · A perfect-square parametric speed
examples.question: Find the length for \(x=t^2\), \(y=t-t^3/3\), 0≤t≤2.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}X^{\prime}=2t,\qquad Y^{\prime}=1-t^2\\\frac{ds}{dt}=\sqrt{4t^2+(1-t^2)^2}=1+t^2\\L=\left[t+\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac{14}{3}\end{gathered}\]

Although Y′ changes sign, speed remains positive. This parametrisation is not a graph with monotone y, but the length formula still applies.

examples.title: 3 · A hyperbolic profile
examples.question: Find the length of \(y=4\cosh(x/4)\) on 0≤x≤4ln2.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y^{\prime}=\sinh(x/4)\\\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}=\cosh(x/4)\\L=4\sinh(\ln2)=3\end{gathered}\]

Cosh is positive, so the principal square root has no sign ambiguity.

examples.title: 4 · A polar spiral
examples.question: Find the length of \(r=3e^{2\theta}\), 0≤θ≤ln2.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}=6e^{2\theta}\\\frac{ds}{d\theta}=3\sqrt5e^{2\theta}\\L=\frac{3\sqrt5}{2}(4-1)=\frac{9\sqrt5}{2}\end{gathered}\]

The exponential is positive throughout. Use polar speed, not the polar area integrand.

lessons.title: Curved surfaces of revolution
lessons.summary: Multiply a small arc length by its circumference.
lessons.objective: Calculate curved surface areas using the distance from the stated rotation axis.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Retain exact values until the final numerical step.
lessons.ideas:
A narrow strip makes a curved band

Rotating an arc element ds at distance ρ from the axis gives dS=2πρ ds. The radius is a distance, so it is non-negative. The result is the curved area; end discs are included only if a question explicitly asks for them.

\[\begin{gathered}S=2\pi\int\rho\,ds\\S_x=2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta|Y(t)|\sqrt{X^{\prime}(t)^2+Y^{\prime}(t)^2}\,dt\\S_y=2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta|X(t)|\sqrt{X^{\prime}(t)^2+Y^{\prime}(t)^2}\,dt\end{gathered}\]

Choose the radius before integrating

About the x-axis use |y|; about the y-axis use |x|. For a horizontal axis y=c, use |y−c|. If that expression changes sign, split at every crossing. An unsplit signed integral can cancel two positive areas.

Simplify the speed first

The derivative squares may combine into a perfect square, especially for hyperbolic or parametric curves. Prove its sign before removing a root. Then integrate radius times speed, which may need a second substitution or a reduction formula.

Check the surface being measured

A parametrisation that retraces an arc can count the same surface more than once. Confirm one traversal of the generating arc and whether distinct bands overlap. Units for surface area are square units. Volume uses discs or shells and has cubic units.
lessons.method:
1. State the axis and the non-negative radius.
  2. Find speed using the arc-length formula.
  3. Split the interval at radius sign changes.
  4. Integrate 2π times radius times speed.
  5. Include only the requested curved surface and check square units.
mistakes: Use distance from the axis rather than a signed coordinate.
The y-axis needs |x|, not |y|.
Do not substitute the volume formula π∫y²dx.
End discs are separate from the curved surface.
A retraced arc can count a surface twice.

examples.title: 1 · A straight generator
examples.question: Rotate \(y=2x\), 0≤x≤3, about the x-axis. Find the curved area.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\rho=2x,\qquad ds=\sqrt5\,dx\\S=4\pi\sqrt5\int_0^3x\,dx=18\pi\sqrt5\end{gathered}\]

This agrees with π times base radius 6 times slant height 3√5. The base disc is not included.

examples.title: 2 · A catenary surface
examples.question: Rotate \(y=2\cosh(x/2)\), 0≤x≤2ln2, about the x-axis.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}S=4\pi\int_0^{2\ln2}\cosh^2(x/2)\,dx\\=4\pi\left[\frac x2+\frac{\sinh x}{2}\right]_0^{2\ln2}\\=4\pi\ln2+\frac{15\pi}{4}\end{gathered}\]

The speed is cosh(x/2), while the radius is twice this value. These are separate factors.

examples.title: 3 · Rotation about the vertical axis
examples.question: Rotate \(x=t^2\), \(y=t-t^3/3\), 0≤t≤1, about the y-axis.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\rho=t^2,\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=1+t^2\\S=2\pi\int_0^1(t^2+t^4)\,dt=\frac{16\pi}{15}\end{gathered}\]

The vertical axis makes x the radius. Inserting y instead would calculate a different surface.

examples.title: 4 · Split where the radius changes sign
examples.question: Rotate \(x=t\), \(y=t-1\), 0≤t≤3, about the x-axis.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}S=2\pi\sqrt2\int_0^3|t-1|\,dt\\=2\pi\sqrt2\left(\int_0^1(1-t)\,dt\\\quad+\int_1^3(t-1)\,dt\right)=5\pi\sqrt2\end{gathered}\]

The two cones occupy different x-intervals, so their curved areas add. A signed radius would incorrectly cancel some area.

lessons.title: Rectangle estimates, sums and limits
lessons.summary: Use monotonicity to justify the direction of every bound.
lessons.objective: Build lower and upper sums, squeeze their limits and justify series comparisons.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Retain exact values until the final numerical step.

Review arithmetic, geometric and power sums and the squeeze principle. Maclaurin estimates appear in one written extension; use the preceding differentiation chapter when needed.
lessons.ideas:
The rectangle width is part of the sum

Divide [a,b] into N equal intervals of width h=(b−a)/N. For a continuous increasing function, left endpoints give the lower sum Lₙ and right endpoints give the upper sum Uₙ. For a decreasing function these choices reverse.

\[\begin{gathered}L_N\le\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\le U_N\\U_N-L_N=h|f(b)-f(a)|\end{gathered}\]

The inequalities are strict when the function is strictly monotone and the intervals have positive width. If h tends to zero, both bounds approach the integral. First rewrite a sum to identify both its sample points and its width.

Unit rectangles compare finite series

For positive decreasing f on [m,N], the left and right unit-width rectangles bound the integral. Isolating endpoints gives useful bounds for the complete finite sum.

\[\begin{gathered}J_N=\int_m^Nf(x)\,dx\\J_N+f(N)\le\sum_{r=m}^Nf(r)\le J_N+f(m)\end{gathered}\]

For increasing f, these endpoint corrections reverse. Prove monotonicity on the whole comparison interval; a function with a maximum may need a later starting point.

Limits do not preserve strictness automatically

Positive increasing partial sums with a uniform upper bound converge. A strict finite-N inequality normally gives only a non-strict bound after taking a limit. To retain strictness, exhibit a fixed positive gap that survives for all later N. To prove divergence, a lower bound tending to infinity is sufficient.

Accuracy thresholds need the right integer

For a gap C/N, a non-strict target allows equality; a strict target does not. Check the proposed least integer and its predecessor. A bound on the gap is different from the actual error of a particular rectangle sum.
lessons.method:
1. Identify width, endpoints and the function represented by the sum.
  2. Prove the required monotonicity on the stated interval.
  3. Draw or describe which rectangles lie above and below.
  4. Simplify the sums or bound their gap, including endpoint terms.
  5. Take limits with justified inequality signs and check integer thresholds.
mistakes: Do not omit the rectangle width.
Right endpoints are upper heights only for an increasing function.
Unit-rectangle comparisons need endpoint corrections.
Strict finite bounds can become non-strict at the limit.
For a strict accuracy target, equality is insufficient.

examples.title: 1 · Exact polynomial rectangle sums
examples.question: Find Lₙ,Uₙ and their common limit for \(f(x)=x^2+x\) on [0,1].
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}f^{\prime}(x)=2x+1>0\\U_N=\frac{(N+1)(5N+1)}{6N^2}\\L_N=\frac{(N-1)(5N-1)}{6N^2}\\U_N-L_N=\frac2N,\qquad\lim L_N=\lim U_N=\frac56\end{gathered}\]

Use sample points r/N and width 1/N, then the formulae for the first and second powers of r.

examples.title: 2 · A strict accuracy target
examples.question: For \(f(x)=5^x\) on [0,1], find the least N with Uₙ−Lₙ<1/500.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}U_N-L_N=\frac{5-1}{N}=\frac4N\\\frac4N<\frac1{500}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N>2000\\N_{\min}=2001\end{gathered}\]

At N=2000 the gap equals the target, which does not satisfy the strict inequality.

examples.title: 3 · A convergent reciprocal series
examples.question: Use \(f(x)=x^{-2}\) on [1,N] to bound \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^Nr^{-2}\), N≥2. Deduce convergence.
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}\int_1^N x^{-2}\,dx=1-\frac1N\\1-\frac1N+\frac1{N^2}The positive partial sums increase and remain bounded by 2. The finite strict comparisons justify non-strict limiting bounds; a stricter claim would require further evidence.

examples.title: 4 · A sum represented by an inverse function
examples.question: Find \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{r=1}^N\frac{N}{N^2+r^2}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{r=1}^N\frac{N}{N^2+r^2}\\=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^N\frac1{1+(r/N)^2}\\\lim R_N=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\frac\pi4\end{gathered}\]

This is a right-endpoint lower sum for a strictly decreasing function. The upper-minus-lower gap is 1/(2N), so both have the same limit.

questions.title: A complete hyperbolic integral
questions.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\int_0^{2}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9+4x^2}}\). Write the answer as A ln q, where q=3. Give A and the exact upper limit in u when x=(a/k)sinh u, written as u=ln q by giving q.
questions.solution_html:
\[\begin{gathered}x=\frac{3}{2}\sinh u,\qquad\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9+4x^2}}=\frac{du}{2}\end{gathered}\]

The limits become 0 and ln q; integrating the constant gives the complete logarithmic result.
questions.hint_html: Write the full integral or identity first. Check the differential, both endpoints and all sign restrictions. Give every requested coefficient or value; these together specify the complete answer.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct upper exponential q.

questions.title: A complete hyperbolic integral
questions.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4+9x^2}}\). Write the answer as A ln q, where q=2. Give A and the exact upper limit in u when x=(a/k)sinh u, written as u=ln q by giving q.
questions.solution_html:
\[\begin{gathered}x=\frac{2}{3}\sinh u,\qquad\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4+9x^2}}=\frac{du}{3}\end{gathered}\]

The limits become 0 and ln q; integrating the constant gives the complete logarithmic result.
questions.hint_html: Write the full integral or identity first. Check the differential, both endpoints and all sign restrictions. Give every requested coefficient or value; these together specify the complete answer.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct upper exponential q.

questions.title: A circular root with its scale
questions.prompt_html: Evaluate \(\int_0^{1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{16-4x^2}}\), exactly.
questions.solution_html:
\[\begin{gathered}\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-k^2x^2}}=\frac1k\sin^{-1}\frac{kx}{a}+C\end{gathered}\]

The upper inverse-sine argument is 1/2 and the lower is zero. Include the factor 1/k.
questions.hint_html: Write the full integral or identity first. Check the differential, both endpoints and all sign restrictions. Give every requested coefficient or value; these together specify the complete answer.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the complete correct complete exact integral.

questions.title: A circular root with its scale

questions.title: A cotangent recurrence and a solid of revolution
questions.prompt_html:
For each non-negative integer \(n\), define

\[I_n=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\cot^n x\,dx.\]

  1. Derive a recurrence expressing \(I_{n+2}\) in terms of \(I_n\).

    [5]

  2. Find \(I_0\) and \(I_2\) exactly.

    [2]

  3. The region under \(y=2\cot^2x\) on this interval is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the power:

\[\frac{d}{dx}(\cot^{n+1}x)=-(n+1)\cot^n x\csc^2x=-(n+1)(\cot^n x+\cot^{n+2}x).\]

At the upper limit the power is zero; at the lower limit it is \(3^{(n+1)/2}\). Thus

\[-3^{(n+1)/2}=-(n+1)(I_n+I_{n+2}).\]

Rearrange to obtain the stated recurrence.

(b)

The interval has length \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Put \(n=0\) into the recurrence:

\[I_2=\sqrt3-I_0=\sqrt3-\frac\pi3.\]

(c)

The disc formula requires the square of the ordinate:

\[V=\pi\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}(2\cot^2x)^2\,dx=4\pi I_4.\]
\[I_4=\frac{3^{3/2}}3-I_2=\frac\pi3.\]
\[V=\frac{4\pi^2}3.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate a power of cotangent and use \(\csc^2x=1+\cot^2x\).

(b)

Start with the integral of 1.

(c)

The volume uses \(I_4\), not \(I_2\).

questions.title: Recovering an exponent from a volume
questions.prompt_html:
For \(a\gt 0\), the curve \(y=3(x/2)^a\) is considered on \(0\le x\le2\).

  1. Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) on this interval.

    [3]

  2. The region under the curve is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Its volume is \(6\pi\). Determine \(a\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The interval length is 2. Hence

\[\bar y=\frac12\int_0^2 3(x/2)^a\,dx=\frac32\cdot\frac{2}{a+1}=\frac3{a+1}.\]

(b)

Using discs,

\[V=\pi\int_0^2 9(x/2)^{2a}\,dx=\frac{18\pi}{2a+1}.\]

Equating this to \(6\pi\) gives \(2a+1=3\), so \(a=1\), which satisfies \(a\gt 0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the integral divided by the interval length.

(b)

Square the function before integrating.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the volume as a function of the exponent.

questions.title: A weighted secant integral
questions.prompt_html:
Let

\[I_n=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sec^n x\tan^2x\,dx\quad(n\ge0).\]

  1. Use \(u=\tan x\) to find \(I_2\).

    [2]

  2. By differentiating \(\sec^{n-2}x\tan^3x\), derive a recurrence linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\) for integers \(n\ge2\).

    [5]

  3. Hence find the mean value of \(\sec^6x\tan^2x\) over the same interval.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[I_2=\int_0^{1/\sqrt3}u^2\,du=\left[\frac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{27}.\]

(b)

\[\frac{d}{dx}(\sec^{n-2}x\tan^3x)=(n-2)\sec^{n-2}x\tan^4x+3\sec^n x\tan^2x.\]

Replace \(\tan^4x\) by \(\tan^2x(\sec^2x-1)\). The derivative becomes

\[(n+1)\sec^n x\tan^2x-(n-2)\sec^{n-2}x\tan^2x.\]

Integration gives the recurrence; the upper boundary is \((2/\sqrt3)^{n-2}/(3\sqrt3)\) and the lower boundary is zero.

(c)

Successive use of the recurrence gives

\[I_4=\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{45},\qquad I_6=\frac{152 \sqrt{3}}{2835}.\]

Divide the integral by the interval length:

\[\text{mean}=\frac6\pi I_6=\frac{304 \sqrt{3}}{945 \pi}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Transform the limits as well as the integrand.

(b)

Keep the boundary term; it is not zero at \(\frac{\pi}{6}\).

(c)

Use both the n=4 and n=6 cases.

questions.title: An inverse-hyperbolic endpoint integral
questions.prompt_html:
1. Evaluate

    \[\int_5^7\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x-2)^2-9}},\]

    giving a logarithmic exact answer. Treat the lower endpoint as a one-sided limit.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=(x-2)/3\). The integral becomes \(\int_1^{5/3}(u^2-1)^{-1/2}\,du\). At \(u=1\) the integrand is unbounded, but \(\cosh^{-1}u\to0\) as \(u\to1^+\).

\[\cosh^{-1}\frac53=\ln\left(\frac53+\frac43\right)=\ln3.\]

An antiderivative on the stated interval is

\[\cosh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \right)}\]

Applying the limits gives

\[\int_{5}^{7} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 9}}\,dx=\ln{\left(3 \right)}.\]

Thus the requested logarithmic value is \(\ln3\).

questions.title: A decaying profile and a volume bisector
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=2e^{-3x}\) for \(0\le x\le1\).

  1. Find the mean value of \(f\,^{\prime}(x)\) on the interval.

    [3]

  2. Find the volume generated by rotating the region under \(y=f(x)\) about the \(x\)-axis.

    [3]

  3. The plane \(x=c\) divides this solid into two equal volumes. Determine \(c\) exactly and explain why it is unique.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[-2 + \frac{2}{e^{3}}\]

(b)

\[\frac{2 \pi \left(1 - e^{-6}\right)}{3}\]

(c)

\[- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{1}{2 e^{6}} + \frac{1}{2} \right)}}{6}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The fundamental theorem gives

\[\frac1{1-0}\int_0^1 f\,^{\prime}(x)\,dx=f(1)-f(0)=2(e^{-3}-1).\]

(b)

\[V=\pi\int_0^1 4e^{-6x}\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{3}(1-e^{-6}).\]

(c)

\[\frac{2\pi}{3}(1-e^{-6c})=\frac12\cdot\frac{2\pi}{3}(1-e^{-6}).\]
\[e^{-6c}=\frac{1+e^{-6}}2,\qquad c=\frac16\ln\frac2{1+e^{-6}}.\]

This value lies between 0 and 1. The accumulated volume has derivative \(4\pi e^{-6c}\gt 0\), so it is strictly increasing and the bisecting value is unique.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate the derivative rather than its magnitude.

(b)

The volume requires f squared.

(c)

Equate the accumulated volume to half the total.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set up the mean of the derivative.

(b)

Now \(x=\frac13\ln(y/2)\) and \(2\le y\le4\). Hence

questions.title: Determining a scale from surface area
questions.prompt_html:
The arc \(y=2\sqrt{x+a}\), \(0\le x\le3\), has \(a\gt 0\).

  1. Show that its surface area about the \(x\)-axis is

    \[S=\frac{8\pi}{3}\left((a+4)^{3/2}-(a+1)^{3/2}\right).\]
    [4]

  2. Verify that \(a=3\) gives \(S=\frac{8\pi}{3}(7\sqrt7-8)\), and show that no other positive \(a\) gives this area.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The radius is positive and \(y^{\prime}=1/\sqrt{x+a}\). Thus

\[y\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}=2\sqrt{x+a+1}.\]
\[S=4\pi\int_0^3\sqrt{x+a+1}\,dx=\frac{8\pi}{3}[(x+a+1)^{3/2}]_0^3.\]

(b)

Substitution gives the required expression. Also

\[\frac{dS}{da}=4\pi(\sqrt{a+4}-\sqrt{a+1})\gt 0.\]

Therefore the surface area is strictly increasing in \(a\), proving uniqueness.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the two square roots before integrating.

(b)

Differentiate the area with respect to the parameter.

questions.title: A sine-power recurrence with scaling
questions.prompt_html:
Define \(I_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n u\,du\) for non-negative integers \(n\).

  1. Prove \((n+2)I_{n+2}=(n+1)I_n\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(I_6\) exactly.

    [3]

  3. For \(k\gt 0\), the region under \(y=3\sin^3(kx)\) on \(0\le x\le\pi/(2k)\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find its volume in terms of \(k\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac d{du}(\sin^{n+1}u\cos u)=(n+1)\sin^n u-(n+2)\sin^{n+2}u.\]

The boundary product is zero at both endpoints. Integrating proves the recurrence.

(b)

\[I_0=\frac\pi2,\quad I_2=\frac\pi4,\quad I_4=\frac{3\pi}{16},\quad I_6=\frac{5\pi}{32}.\]

(c)

\[V=9\pi\int_0^{\pi/(2k)}\sin^6(kx)\,dx=\frac{9\pi}{k}I_6=\frac{45\pi^2}{32k}.\]
questions.hint_html:

questions.title: An exponential recurrence with a four-step index
questions.prompt_html:
For non-negative integers \(n\), let

\[I_n=\int_{0}^{1} x^{n} e^{2 x^{4}}\,dx.\]

  1. Evaluate \(I_3\) using \(u=2x^4\).

    [2]

  2. For integers \(n\ge4\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-4}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 3} e^{2 x^{4}}\).

    [4]

  3. Hence find the exact value of \(I_{11}\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[- \frac{1}{8} + \frac{e^{2}}{8}\]

(b)

\[8 I_{n} + I_{n-4} \left(n - 3\right) = e^{2}\]

(c)

\[- \frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[I_3=\frac18\int_0^2e^u\,du=\frac{e^2-1}{8}.\]

(b)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 3} e^{2 x^{4}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=8 x^{3} x^{n - 3} e^{2 x^{4}} + \frac{x^{n - 3} \left(n - 3\right) e^{2 x^{4}}}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=8 x^{n} e^{2 x^{4}} + x^{n - 4} \left(n - 3\right) e^{2 x^{4}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[8 I_{n} + I_{n-4} \left(n - 3\right) = e^{2}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(e^{2}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{3}=- \frac{1}{8} + \frac{e^{2}}{8}.\]
\[I_{7}=\frac{e^{2}-\left(4\right)\left(- \frac{1}{8} + \frac{e^{2}}{8}\right)}{8}=\frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}.\]
\[I_{11}=\frac{e^{2}-\left(8\right)\left(\frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}\right)}{8}=- \frac{1}{16} + \frac{e^{2}}{16}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The differential is \(du=8x^3\,dx\).

(b)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(c)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.

questions.title: Two integrations by parts with inverse powers
questions.prompt_html:
For positive integers \(n\), define

\[I_n=\int_1^2x^{-n}\sin\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx.\]

  1. Prove the recurrence

    \[n(n+1)I_{n+2}=n+\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}-\frac{\pi^2}{4}I_n.\]
    [5]

  2. Express \(I_5\) in terms of \(I_1\) and \(\pi\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate \(I_{n+2}\) by parts, integrating the inverse power first:

\[I_{n+2}=\frac1{n+1}+\frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}\int_1^2x^{-n-1}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx.\]

A second integration by parts gives

\[\int_1^2x^{-n-1}\cos\frac{\pi x}{2}\,dx=\frac{2^{-n}}n-\frac\pi{2n}I_n.\]

Substitute this into the first equation and multiply by \(n(n+1)\) to obtain the required identity.

(b)

\[2I_3=1+\frac\pi4-\frac{\pi^2}4I_1,\qquad 12I_5=3+\frac\pi{16}-\frac{\pi^2}4I_3.\]

Eliminating \(I_3\) gives

\[I_5=\frac{\pi^{4} I_{1}}{384} - \frac{\pi^{2}}{96} - \frac{\pi^{3}}{384} + \frac{\pi}{192} + \frac{1}{4}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Track the sine and cosine values at both 1 and 2.

(b)

Apply the recurrence at n=1 and n=3.

questions.title: A weighted cosine family and volume
questions.prompt_html:
Define

\[I_n=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}e^{3x}\cos^n x\,dx\quad(n\ge0).\]

  1. Evaluate \(I_0\) and show that \(I_1=\frac1{10}(e^{3\pi/2}+e^{-3\pi/2})\).

    [3]

  2. For integers \(n\ge2\), derive \((n^2+9)I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}\).

    [6]

  3. The region under \(y=e^{3x/2}\cos^2x\) on \(-\pi/2\le x\le\pi/2\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[I_0=- \frac{1}{3 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{3},\qquad I_1=\frac1{10}(e^{3\pi/2}+e^{-3\pi/2}).\]

(b)

\[(n^2+9)I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}\]

(c)

\[\frac{16 \pi \sinh{\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2} \right)}}{325}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The first is a direct exponential integral. For the second, two integrations by parts give

\[\int e^{3x}\cos x\,dx=\frac{e^{3x}}{10}(3\cos x+\sin x).\]

At the endpoints cosine is zero, giving

\[I_1=\frac1{10}(e^{3\pi/2}+e^{-3\pi/2}).\]

(b)

Write \(J=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} e^{3x}\sin x\cos^{n-1}x\,dx\). Integrating \(I_n\) by parts gives \(3I_n=nJ\) because the cosine-power boundary term vanishes. Integrate \(J\) by parts in the same way. Since \(n\ge2\), its boundary term also vanishes, and

\[3J=-I_n+(n-1)\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}e^{3x}\sin^2x\cos^{n-2}x\,dx.\]

Use \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\) and eliminate \(J\):

\[9I_n=n(n-1)I_{n-2}-n^2I_n.\]

Rearrangement proves the formula.

(c)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=- \frac{1}{3 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{3}.\]
\[I_{2}=- \frac{2}{39 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{2 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{39}.\]
\[I_{4}=- \frac{8}{325 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}} + \frac{8 e^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}}{325}.\]

Finally include the scale factor required by the application:

\[\piI_{4}=\frac{16 \pi \sinh{\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2} \right)}}{325}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the elementary antiderivative for an exponential times cosine.

(b)

(c)

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\left(2 - n\right) \operatorname{sech}^{n - 2}{\left(x \right)} + \left(n - 1\right) \operatorname{sech}^{n}{\left(x \right)}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[I_{n} \left(n - 1\right) + I_{n-2} \left(2 - n\right) = \frac{3 \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{n - 2}}{5}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(\frac{3 \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{n - 2}}{5}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{2}=\frac{3}{5}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{\frac{48}{125}-\left(-2\right)\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}{3}=\frac{66}{125}.\]
\[I_{6}=\frac{\frac{768}{3125}-\left(-4\right)\left(\frac{66}{125}\right)}{5}=\frac{7368}{15625}.\]

questions.title: A quadratic-root family and a parabola
questions.prompt_html:
For integer \(n\), define \(I_n=\int_0^4(9+x^2)^{n/2}\,dx\).

  1. Find \(I_{-1}\) in logarithmic form.

    [3]

  2. For integers \(n\in\mathbb Z\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x \left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{n}{2}}\).

    [4]

  3. The curve \(y=x^2/6\) is restricted to \(0\le x\le4\). Show that its length is \(I_1/3\) and evaluate that length exactly.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\ln{\left(3 \right)}\]

(b)

\[I_{n} \left(n + 1\right) - 9 I_{n-2} n = 4 \cdot 5^{n}\]

(c)

\[\frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2} + \frac{10}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

questions.title: Bounding e squared using a positive integral
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{1} \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\,dx\).

  1. For integers \(n\ge1\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-1}\). You may consider the derivative of \(\left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\).

    [4]

  2. Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).

    [3]

  3. Show that \(0\lt I_{4}\lt \frac{1}{3}\) and hence prove

    \[7\lt e^{2}\lt \frac{67}{9}.\]
    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[2 I_{n} - I_{n-1} n = -1\]

(b)

\[- \frac{21}{4} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}\]

(c)

\[7\lt e^{2}\lt \frac{67}{9}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=\left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{n \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}}{1 - x} + 2 \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- n \left(1 - x\right)^{n - 1} e^{2 x} + 2 \left(1 - x\right)^{n} e^{2 x}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[2 I_{n} - I_{n-1} n = -1\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(-1\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

Evaluate the initial integral directly, then apply the reduction formula at each successive index:

\[I_{0}=- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{2}}{2}.\]
\[I_{1}=\frac{-1-\left(-1\right)\left(- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{e^{2}}{2}\right)}{2}=- \frac{3}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{-1-\left(-2\right)\left(- \frac{3}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}\right)}{2}=- \frac{5}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}.\]
\[I_{3}=\frac{-1-\left(-3\right)\left(- \frac{5}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}\right)}{2}=- \frac{19}{8} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{8}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{-1-\left(-4\right)\left(- \frac{19}{8} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{8}\right)}{2}=- \frac{21}{4} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}.\]

(c)

For \(0\lt x\lt 1\), the function \(e^{2x}(1-x)^{2}\) is strictly decreasing from 1, because its logarithmic derivative is \(2-2/(1-x)\lt 0\). Thus

\[0\lt (1-x)^{4}e^{2x}\lt (1-x)^{2}.\]

Integrating gives \(0\lt I_{4}\lt \frac{1}{3}\). Insert \(I_{4}=- \frac{21}{4} + \frac{3 e^{2}}{4}\) and divide by the positive exponential coefficient to obtain the bounds.

  2. Prove by induction that \(I_n=A_ne^6+B_n\) for every non-negative integer \(n\), where \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are rational. State recurrences for these coefficients.

    [4]

(a)

\[3 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = 2^{n} e^{6}\]

(b)

\[A_0=\frac13,\quad B_0=-\frac13,\qquad A_n=\frac{2^n-nA_{n-1}}3,\quad B_n=-\frac n3B_{n-1}.\]

(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{3} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}}{\ln{\left(x \right)}} + 3 x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=n x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n - 1} + 3 x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)}^{n}.\]

\[I_{k+1}=\frac{2^{k+1}e^6-(k+1)(A_ke^6+B_k)}3.\]

\[H^{\prime}(x)=\frac{n x^{n} e^{- 2 x}}{x} - 2 x^{n} e^{- 2 x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=n x^{n - 1} e^{- 2 x} - 2 x^{n} e^{- 2 x}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[- 2 I_{n} + I_{n-1} n = \frac{2^{n}}{e^{4}}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(\frac{2^{n}}{e^{4}}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The integrand is positive on the interior, so \(I_n\gt 0\). Also \(I_0=(1-e^{-4})/2\lt 1/2\). Suppose \(I_k\lt k!/2^{k+1}\). The recurrence gives

\[I_{k+1}=\frac{k+1}{2}I_k-2^ke^{-4}\lt \frac{k+1}{2}\frac{k!}{2^{k+1}}=\frac{(k+1)!}{2^{k+2}}.\]

Thus the claim holds at the next index; induction proves it for all non-negative integers.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

The subtracted boundary term makes the inequality strict.

marking_criteria.description_html: Rearrange the derivative into the two integrands.

questions.title: A truncated circular-root family
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}} \frac{x^{n}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}}\,dx\).

  1. For integers \(n\ge2\), derive a reduction formula linking \(I_n\) and \(I_{n-2}\). You may consider the derivative of \(x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}}\).

    [5]

  2. Hence find the exact value of \(I_{4}\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[- I_{n} n + I_{n-2} \left(9 n - 9\right) = 2^{- n} 3^{n + \frac{1}{2}}\]

(b)

\[- \frac{567 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{81 \pi}{16}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(H(x)=x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}}\). The product and chain rules give

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{x x^{n - 1}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}} + \frac{x^{n - 1} \sqrt{9 - x^{2}} \left(n - 1\right)}{x}.\]

Collect the powers of the common factor. This can be written as

\[H^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{n x^{n}}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}} + \frac{x^{n - 2} \left(9 n - 9\right)}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}}.\]

Integrating between the stated endpoints gives

\[- I_{n} n + I_{n-2} \left(9 n - 9\right) = 2^{- n} 3^{n + \frac{1}{2}}\]

Here the endpoint difference is \(2^{- n} 3^{n + \frac{1}{2}}\). The stated index restriction ensures that all terms used in this recurrence are defined.

(b)

The initial value is I₀=[sin⁻¹(x/3)]₀^(3/2)=π/6. Keep the nonzero upper boundary term when reducing:

\[I_{0}=\frac{\pi}{6}.\]
\[I_{2}=\frac{\frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{4}-\left(9\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)}{-2}=- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{8} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}.\]
\[I_{4}=\frac{\frac{81 \sqrt{3}}{16}-\left(27\right)\left(- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{8} + \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)}{-4}=- \frac{567 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{81 \pi}{16}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the suggested derivative, express it using the two required integrands, and retain both endpoint terms.

(b)

Identify the correct initial index and do not skip an intermediate recurrence step.

marking_criteria.description_html: Rearrange the derivative into the two integrands.
Apply the recurrence at the needed indices.

questions.title: A hyperbolic parametrisation of a circular surface
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad y=3 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}.\]

  1. Show that \(ds/dt=6\operatorname{sech}(2t)\) and set up the surface integral about the \(x\)-axis.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[x^{\prime}=-6\operatorname{sech}(2t)\tanh(2t),\qquad y^{\prime}=6\operatorname{sech}^2(2t).\]

Using \(\tanh^2v+\operatorname{sech}^2v=1\), the squared speed is \(36\operatorname{sech}^2(2t)\). Both the speed and radius are nonnegative, giving the stated integral.

(b)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}}\left(3 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=- 6 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)} \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=6 - 6 \tanh^{2}{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=6 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(18 \tanh{\left(2 t \right)} \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}\right)\,dt=- 9 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[- 9 \operatorname{sech}{\left(2 t \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}}=\frac{18 \pi}{5}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: An exponential arc with a perfect-square speed
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=- 4 t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2},\qquad y=4 e^{t},\qquad 0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=e^{2 t} - 4,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=4 e^{t}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\left(e^{2 t} + 4\right)^{2}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}e^{2 t} + 4\,dt=\left[4 t + \frac{e^{2 t}}{2}\right]_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}=\frac{3}{2} + 4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

marking_criteria.description_html: Simplify the speed and choose the correct sign.

questions.title: A half-cycloid surface of revolution
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 t - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=3 - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)},\qquad 0\le t\le \pi.\]

  1. Show that the surface area about the \(x\)-axis can be written as \(72\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^3(t/2)\,dt\).

    [4]

  2. Evaluate this surface area exactly.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[(x^{\prime})^2+(y^{\prime})^2=9(1-\cos t)^2+9\sin^2t=36\sin^2(t/2).\]

On \(0\le t\le\pi\), sine of the half-angle is nonnegative. Since \(y=6\sin^2(t/2)\), multiplying the radius, speed and \(2\pi\) gives the required integral.

(b)

Put \(u=t/2\). Then

\[\int_0^\pi\sin^3(t/2)\,dt=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin u(1-\cos^2u)\,du=\frac43.\]
\[S=72\pi\cdot\frac43=96\pi.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Rewrite 1−cos t using the half-angle.

(b)

Integrate sin u(1−cos²u).

questions.title: Two substitutions for an exponential surface
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(y=\tfrac12e^{2x}\) is considered for \(- \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}\le x\le- \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2} + \ln{\left(2 \right)}\).

  1. Use \(u=e^{2x}\) to show that the surface area about the \(x\)-axis is \(\frac\pi2\int_{3/4}^{4/3}\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du\).

    [3]

  2. Now use \(u=\sinh v\) to evaluate the area, giving a logarithmic exact answer.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Here \(y^{\prime}=e^{2x}=u\), \(y=u/2\) and \(dx=du/(2u)\). Substitute all three factors into \(2\pi\int y\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}\,dx\) to obtain the result.

(b)

The new limits are \(v=\ln2\) and \(v=\ln3\). The integral becomes \(\int\cosh^2v\,dv\), with antiderivative \(v/2+\sinh(2v)/4\). Equivalently,

\[\int\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du=\frac12\left(u\sqrt{1+u^2}+\sinh^{-1}u\right).\]
\[S=\frac\pi4\left(\frac{20}9-\frac{15}{16}+\ln\frac32\right)=\frac\pi4\left(\frac{185}{144}+\ln\frac32\right).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Transform radius, speed and differential separately.

(b)

The two inverse hyperbolic values simplify to ln2 and ln3.

questions.title: A hyperbolic substitution for a parabolic surface
questions.prompt_html:
The arc \(y=x^2/4\), \(0\le x\le3/2\), is rotated once about the \(x\)-axis.

  1. Prove \(\sinh^2u\cosh^2u=(\cosh4u-1)/8\) using double-angle identities.

    [3]

  2. Use \(x=2\sinh u\) to express the surface area as an integral of \(\sinh^2u\cosh^2u\).

    [5]

  3. Hence find the exact area in terms of \(\pi\) and \(\ln2\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sinh^2u\cosh^2u=\frac14\sinh^2(2u)=\frac18(\cosh4u-1).\]

(b)

The surface formula gives

\[S=2\pi\int_0^{3/2}\frac{x^2}{4}\sqrt{1+\frac{x^2}4}\,dx.\]

Now \(dx=2\cosh u\,du\), \(\sqrt{1+x^2/4}=\cosh u\), and the upper limit is \(\sinh^{-1}(3/4)=\ln2\). Collecting the factors gives the result.

(c)

\[S=\frac\pi2\int_0^{\ln2}(\cosh4u-1)\,du=\left[\frac\pi8\sinh4u-\frac\pi2u\right]_0^{\ln2}.\]

Since \(\sinh(4\ln2)=(16-1/16)/2=255/32\),

\[S=\frac{255\pi}{256}-\frac\pi2\ln2.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the double-angle formula twice.

(b)

Use the positive branch of cosh.

(c)

Use the identity from part (a) before integrating.

questions.title: A catenary surface and its local expansion
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(y=\tfrac14(e^{2x}+e^{-2x})\) for \(0\le x\le\tfrac12\ln2\).

  1. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [5]

  2. Find the Maclaurin expansion of \(y\) up to and including \(x^2\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}}\left(\frac{\cosh{\left(2 t \right)}}{2}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\sinh{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\cosh{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(\frac{\cosh^{2}{\left(2 t \right)}}{2}\right)\,dt=\frac{t}{4} + \frac{\sinh{\left(4 t \right)}}{16}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{t}{4} + \frac{\sinh{\left(4 t \right)}}{16}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}}=\frac{\pi \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{4} + \frac{15 \pi}{64}.\]

(b)

\[\frac14[(1+2x+2x^2+\cdots)+(1-2x+2x^2+\cdots)]=\frac12+x^2+O(x^4).\]

The odd powers cancel because the function is even.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

(b)

Expand both exponentials before adding.

marking_criteria.description_html: Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: A nontrivial hyperbolic parametrisation
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 \cosh{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=\frac{17 t}{8} - \frac{9 \sinh{\left(2 t \right)}}{16},\qquad 0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]

  1. Show that \(dy/dt=1-\tfrac94\sinh^2t\) and find \(ds/dt\).

    [4]

  2. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [9]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate and use \(\cosh2t=1+2\sinh^2t\):

\[y^{\prime}=\frac{17}8-\frac98\cosh2t=1-\frac94\sinh^2t.\]
\[(x^{\prime})^2+(y^{\prime})^2=9\sinh^2t+\left(1-\frac94\sinh^2t\right)^2=\left(1+\frac94\sinh^2t\right)^2.\]

Take the positive root.

(b)

The ordinate is nonnegative: its derivative decreases from 1 to −17/64, so its minimum is at an endpoint; y(0)=0 and y(ln2)>0. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(\frac{17 t}{8} - \frac{9 \sinh{\left(2 t \right)}}{16}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=3 \sinh{\left(t \right)},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{17}{8} - \frac{9 \cosh{\left(2 t \right)}}{8},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac{9 \sinh^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{4} + 1.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(\frac{153 t \sinh^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{32} + \frac{17 t}{8} - \frac{81 \sinh^{2}{\left(t \right)} \sinh{\left(2 t \right)}}{64} - \frac{9 \sinh{\left(2 t \right)}}{16}\right)\,dt=- \frac{17 t^{2}}{128} + \frac{153 t \sinh{\left(2 t \right)}}{128} - \frac{9 \cosh{\left(2 t \right)}}{16} - \frac{81 \cosh{\left(4 t \right)}}{1024}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[- \frac{17 t^{2}}{128} + \frac{153 t \sinh{\left(2 t \right)}}{128} - \frac{9 \cosh{\left(2 t \right)}}{16} - \frac{81 \cosh{\left(4 t \right)}}{1024}\right]_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}=- \frac{38961 \pi}{16384} - \frac{17 \pi \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2}}{64} + \frac{2295 \pi \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{512}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Complete a square in sinh²t.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: A rotated hyperbolic profile and symmetry
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=4 t + 3 \cosh{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=- 3 t + 4 \cosh{\left(t \right)},\qquad -1\le t\le 1.\]

  1. Show that \(ds/dt=5\cosh t\).

    [4]

  2. Explain why the radius for rotation about the \(y\)-axis is \(x\) throughout the arc, and show that the surface area is \(30\pi\int_{-1}^1\cosh^2t\,dt\).

    [4]

  3. Evaluate the surface area exactly in exponential form.

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[(3\sinh t+4)^2+(4\sinh t-3)^2=25(1+\sinh^2t)=25\cosh^2t.\]

Since \(\cosh t\gt 0\), take the positive root.

(b)

On this interval, \(x^{\prime}=3\sinh t+4\ge4-3\sinh1\gt 0\), since \(\sinh1\approx1.1752\). The minimum radius occurs at t=−1, where \(x(-1)=3\cosh1-4\approx0.6292\gt 0\). Therefore x is positive throughout. The surface integral is

\[S=10\pi\int_{-1}^1(3\cosh t+4t)\cosh t\,dt.\]

The \(t\cosh t\) term is odd and integrates to zero.

(c)

\[\int_{-1}^1\cosh^2t\,dt=\left[\frac t2+\frac14\sinh2t\right]_{-1}^1=1+\frac12\sinh2.\]

Therefore

\[S=30\pi+15\pi\sinh2=30\pi+\frac{15\pi}{2}(e^2-e^{-2}).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The cross terms cancel on expansion.

(b)

Use both the sign of the radius and parity of the integrand.

(c)

Use cosh²t=(1+cosh2t)/2.

questions.title: An intersection that determines an arc endpoint
questions.prompt_html:
The curves \(C_1:y=2\cosh(x/2)\) and \(C_2:y=3\sinh x\) are considered for real \(x\).

  1. Show that they intersect at a unique point with \(x=a=2\ln\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}3\).

    [4]

  2. Sketch both curves on the same axes, indicating the intercepts and their intersection.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact length of \(C_1\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=a\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=2\ln\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}3\]

(b)

The intercepts are \((0,2)\) and \((0,0)\); the intersection is \((a,2\sqrt{10}/3)\).

(c)

\[\frac{2}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\sinh x=2\sinh(x/2)\cosh(x/2)\), the intersection equation becomes

\[2\cosh(x/2)=6\sinh(x/2)\cosh(x/2).\]

Divide by the strictly positive cosh factor: \(\sinh(x/2)=1/3\). The sinh function is strictly increasing, so the solution is unique, and its inverse logarithmic form gives the stated value.

(b)

The cosh curve is even with minimum \((0,2)\). The sinh curve is odd and strictly increasing through the origin. It is below the first curve for \(x\lt a\) and above it for \(x\gt a\). Mark the unique intersection \((a,2\sqrt{10}/3)\).

(c)

Here \(y^{\prime}=\sinh(x/2)\), so \(\sqrt{1+(y^{\prime})^2}=\cosh(x/2)\). Thus

\[L=\int_0^a\cosh(x/2)\,dx=2\sinh(a/2)=\frac23.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the double-angle identity and do not divide by sinh.

(b)

Use symmetry and the fact that the intersection is unique.

(c)

The speed is cosh(x/2), and the endpoint sinh is already known.

marking_criteria.description_html: Indicate the unique intersection and relative positions.

questions.title: A scaled catenary surface
questions.prompt_html:
The arc \(y=3\cosh(x/3)\), \(0\le x\le3\ln2\), is rotated about the \(x\)-axis.

  1. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(3 \cosh{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\sinh{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\cosh{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(3 \cosh^{2}{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}\right)\,dt=\frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{9 \sinh{\left(\frac{2 t}{3} \right)}}{4}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{3 t}{2} + \frac{9 \sinh{\left(\frac{2 t}{3} \right)}}{4}\right]_{0}^{3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}=9 \pi \ln{\left(2 \right)} + \frac{135 \pi}{16}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: A derivative average and an exact surface
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=- t^{2} + 8 t,\qquad y=\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3},\qquad 0\le t\le 2.\]

For derivative calculations use \(0\lt t\lt 2\); endpoint values are interpreted by limits.

  1. Find \(dy/dx\) and \(d^2y/dx^2\) in terms of \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Find the mean value of \(d^2y/dx^2\) with respect to \(x\) over the whole arc.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{4 \sqrt{t}}{t - 4},\qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{- t - 4}{\sqrt{t} \left(t - 4\right)^{3}}\]

(b)

\[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\]

(c)

\[\frac{19456 \sqrt{2} \pi}{105}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

First divide the parameter derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{8\sqrt t}{8-2t}=\frac{4\sqrt t}{4-t}.\]

Differentiate this ratio with respect to \(t\) and divide again by \(dx/dt=8-2t\). This gives

\[\frac{- t - 4}{\sqrt{t} \left(t - 4\right)^{3}}\]

(b)

The average of the second derivative is the endpoint change in the first derivative divided by the interval length:

\[\text{mean}=\frac{[dy/dx]_{t=0}^{t=2}}{x(2)-x(0)}=\frac{2\sqrt2-0}{12}=\frac{\sqrt2}{6}.\]

(c)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{2}\left(\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=8 - 2 t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=8 \sqrt{t},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=2 t + 8.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(\frac{32 t^{\frac{5}{2}}}{3} + \frac{128 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\,dt=\frac{64 t^{\frac{5}{2}} \left(5 t + 28\right)}{105}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{64 t^{\frac{5}{2}} \left(5 t + 28\right)}{105}\right]_{0}^{2}=\frac{19456 \sqrt{2} \pi}{105}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The second derivative requires another division by dx/dt.

(b)

Integrate the derivative via its endpoint values.

(c)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the endpoint change in the first derivative.
Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: A cardioid: area, length and an arc bisector
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(a\gt 0\). A polar curve is given by \(r=a(1+\cos\theta)\) for \(-\pi\le\theta\le\pi\).

  1. Sketch the curve and state its maximum distance from the pole.

    [3]

  2. Find its enclosed area.

    [3]

  3. Find the length of the upper half of the curve, from \(\theta=0\) to \(\theta=\pi\).

    [4]

  4. Find the angle \(\alpha\) which bisects this upper-half arc by length, measured from \(\theta=0\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

A right-facing cardioid, symmetric about the initial line; maximum radius \(2a\).

(b)

\[\frac32\pi a^2\]

(c)

\[4a\]

(d)

\[\alpha=\frac\pi3\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The pole occurs at \(\theta=\pm\pi\). The largest radius is \(2a\) at \(\theta=0\). The points at \(\theta=\pm\pi/2\) have radius \(a\). These features determine the sketch.

(b)

\[A=\frac12\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}a^2(1+\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac12a^2(2\pi+0+\pi)=\frac32\pi a^2.\]

(c)

\[\sqrt{r^2+(dr/d\theta)^2}=a\sqrt{2+2\cos\theta}=2a\cos(\theta/2).\]

The cosine is nonnegative on this interval. Therefore

\[L=2a\int_0^\pi\cos(\theta/2)\,d\theta=4a.\]

(d)

\[2a\int_0^\alpha\cos(\theta/2)\,d\theta=2a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin(\alpha/2)=\frac12.\]

Because \(0\le\alpha\le\pi\), the unique solution is \(\alpha=\pi/3\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use symmetry and the values at multiples of π/2.

(b)

Use the polar area formula and symmetry.

(c)

Choose the nonnegative half-angle square root.

(d)

Half the arc length is not generally half the angle.

questions.title: Four integral measures of a catenary
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(y=2\cosh(x/2)\) on \(0\le x\le2\ln3\).

  1. Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) over the corresponding \(x\)-interval.

    [3]

  2. Find the volume obtained by rotating the region under the curve about the \(x\)-axis.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [3]

  4. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{8}{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}\]

(b)

\[4\pi\ln3+\frac{80\pi}{9}\]

(c)

\[\frac{8}{3}\]

(d)

\[4 \pi \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \frac{80 \pi}{9}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The \(x\)-coordinate increases over this interval. Its total change is \(2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}\). Thus

\[\bar y=\frac1{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}\int_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}2 \cosh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\,dt=\frac1{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}\left[4 \sinh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\right]_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}=\frac{8}{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}.\]

(b)

\[V=4\pi\int_0^{2\ln3}\cosh^2(x/2)\,dx=2\pi[x+\sinh x]_0^{2\ln3}=4\pi\ln3+\frac{80\pi}{9}.\]

(c)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\sinh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\cosh^{2}{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}\cosh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\,dt=\left[2 \sinh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\right]_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}=\frac{8}{3}.\]

(d)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}\left(2 \cosh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\sinh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\cosh{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(2 \cosh^{2}{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\right)\,dt=t + \sinh{\left(t \right)}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[t + \sinh{\left(t \right)}\right]_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}=4 \pi \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \frac{80 \pi}{9}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Include dx/dt and divide by the change in x, not the change in t.

(b)

Use cosh²(x/2)=(1+cosh x)/2.

(c)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(d)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

questions.title: Fractional powers with an exact speed
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=\frac{2 t^{\frac{7}{2}}}{7} - 2 \sqrt{t},\qquad y=t^{2},\qquad 1\le t\le 4.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=t^{\frac{5}{2}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=2 t.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\left(t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\right)^{2}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{1}^{4}t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,dt=\left[\frac{2 \sqrt{t} \left(t^{3} + 7\right)}{7}\right]_{1}^{4}=\frac{268}{7}.\]

(b)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{1}^{4}\left(t^{2}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=t^{\frac{5}{2}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=2 t,\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(t^{\frac{9}{2}} + t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\,dt=\frac{2 t^{\frac{5}{2}} \left(5 t^{3} + 11\right)}{55}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{2 t^{\frac{5}{2}} \left(5 t^{3} + 11\right)}{55}\right]_{1}^{4}=\frac{42304 \pi}{55}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

questions.title: An exponential arc with reversed horizontal motion
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=- 9 t + e^{t} + 8,\qquad y=12 e^{\frac{t}{2}},\qquad 0\le t\le 2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [5]

  2. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=e^{t} - 9,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=6 e^{\frac{t}{2}}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\left(e^{t} + 9\right)^{2}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}e^{t} + 9\,dt=\left[9 t + e^{t}\right]_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}=3 + 18 \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\]

(b)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(12 e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=e^{t} - 9,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=6 e^{\frac{t}{2}},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=e^{t} + 9.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(12 e^{\frac{3 t}{2}} + 108 e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)\,dt=8 \left(e^{t} + 27\right) e^{\frac{t}{2}}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[8 \left(e^{t} + 27\right) e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right]_{0}^{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}=544 \pi.\]

(a)

questions.title: A cubic parametric arc and its surface
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=2 t^{2},\qquad y=- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} + 2 t,\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{1}{2}.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=4 t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=2 - 2 t^{2}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\left(2 t^{2} + 2\right)^{2}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}2 t^{2} + 2\,dt=\left[\frac{2 t \left(t^{2} + 3\right)}{3}\right]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{13}{12}.\]

(b)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} + 2 t\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=4 t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=2 - 2 t^{2},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=2 t^{2} + 2.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(- \frac{4 t^{5}}{3} + \frac{8 t^{3}}{3} + 4 t\right)\,dt=\frac{2 t^{2} \left(- t^{4} + 3 t^{2} + 9\right)}{9}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{2 t^{2} \left(- t^{4} + 3 t^{2} + 9\right)}{9}\right]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{155 \pi}{144}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

questions.title: A root parametrisation and two integral measures
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=t^{2},\qquad y=\sqrt{3 - t},\qquad 0\le t\le 3.\]

Derivatives are required only for \(0\lt t\lt 3\).

  1. Find \(d^2y/dx^2\) in terms of \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) over the corresponding \(x\)-interval.

    [5]

  3. Find the volume of the solid formed by rotating the region under this curve about the \(x\)-axis.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{3 \left(2 - t\right)}{16 t^{3} \left(3 - t\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\]

(b)

\[\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{15}\]

(c)

\[9 \pi\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{1}{4 t \sqrt{3 - t}}.\]

Differentiate with respect to t and divide by \(2t\):

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{3 \left(2 - t\right)}{16 t^{3} \left(3 - t\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]

(b)

The \(x\)-coordinate increases over this interval. Its total change is \(9\). Thus

\[\bar y=\frac1{9}\int_{0}^{3}2 t \sqrt{3 - t}\,dt=\frac1{9}\left[\frac{4 \left(3 - t\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5} - 4 \left(3 - t\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{0}^{3}=\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{15}.\]

(c)

\[V=\pi\int_0^3(3-t)\,2t\,dt=\pi[3t^2-\tfrac23t^3]_0^3=9\pi.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Do not substitute an endpoint into a derivative formula that is only valid in the interior.

(b)

Include dx/dt and divide by the change in x, not the change in t.

(c)

Square y before substituting dx=2t dt.

questions.title: Symmetric power coordinates and a mean
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=\frac{4 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 5 t,\qquad y=- \frac{4 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 5 t,\qquad 0\le t\le 4.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [6]

  2. Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) over the corresponding \(x\)-interval.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=2 \sqrt{t} + 5,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=5 - 2 \sqrt{t}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=8 t + 50.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{4}\sqrt{8 t + 50}\,dt=\left[\frac{\sqrt{2} \left(4 t + 25\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}\right]_{0}^{4}=- \frac{125 \sqrt{2}}{6} + \frac{41 \sqrt{82}}{6}.\]

(b)

The \(x\)-coordinate increases over this interval. Its total change is \(\frac{92}{3}\). Thus

\[\bar y=\frac1{\frac{92}{3}}\int_{0}^{4}\left(2 \sqrt{t} + 5\right) \left(- \frac{4 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 5 t\right)\,dt=\frac1{\frac{92}{3}}\left[\frac{4 t^{\frac{5}{2}}}{3} - \frac{8 t^{3}}{9} + \frac{25 t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{4}=\frac{418}{69}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(b)

Include dx/dt and divide by the change in x, not the change in t.

questions.title: A parametrised arc with a polar interpretation
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 - 9 t^{2},\qquad y=3 t \left(1 - 3 t^{2}\right),\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(y\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [4]

  3. Show that the polar form is \(r=3\sec\theta(1-3\tan^2\theta)\) and state the angular interval.

    [3]

  4. Find the area bounded by the arc and the initial line.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[2 \sqrt{3}\]

(b)

\[\frac{32 \sqrt{3} \pi}{5}\]

(c)

\[r=3\sec\theta(1-3\tan^2\theta),\qquad0\le\theta\le\pi/6\]

(d)

\[\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{5}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=- 18 t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=3 - 27 t^{2}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\left(27 t^{2} + 3\right)^{2}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}27 t^{2} + 3\,dt=\left[9 t^{3} + 3 t\right]_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}=2 \sqrt{3}.\]

(b)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}\left(3 - 9 t^{2}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=- 18 t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=3 - 27 t^{2},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=27 t^{2} + 3.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(- 243 t^{4} + 54 t^{2} + 9\right)\,dt=- \frac{243 t^{5}}{5} + 18 t^{3} + 9 t+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[- \frac{243 t^{5}}{5} + 18 t^{3} + 9 t\right]_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}=\frac{32 \sqrt{3} \pi}{5}.\]

(c)

Away from the pole, \(y/x=t\), so \(t=\tan\theta\). Then \(r\cos\theta=3(1-3\tan^2\theta)\). Divide by positive cosine. Since \(0\le t\le1/\sqrt3\), the interval is \(0\le\theta\le\pi/6\); the upper endpoint is the pole by continuity.

(d)

The x-coordinate decreases from 3 to 0. Therefore

\[A=-\int_0^{1/\sqrt3}y(t)x^{\prime}(t)\,dt=54\int_0^{1/\sqrt3}(t^2-3t^4)\,dt=\frac{4\sqrt3}{5}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

(c)

Use y/x before substituting the polar expressions.

(d)

Reverse the sign because x decreases along the parametrisation.
