questions.title: A logarithmic arc on an asymmetric interval
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is \(y=-3\ln(1-x^2/9)\) for \(-1\le x\le2\).

  1. Show that \(ds/dx=(9+x^2)/(9-x^2)\) and express this as partial fractions plus a constant.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiation gives \(y^{\prime}=6x/(9-x^2)\). Thus

\[1+(y^{\prime})^2=\left(\frac{9+x^2}{9-x^2}\right)^2.\]

The denominator is positive on the given interval, so the positive speed is the displayed quotient. Splitting the quotient gives \(3/(3-x)+3/(3+x)-1\).

(b)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{2 t}{3 \left(1 - \frac{t^{2}}{9}\right)}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\frac{\left(t^{2} + 9\right)^{2}}{\left(9 - t^{2}\right)^{2}}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{-1}^{2}\frac{t^{2} + 9}{9 - t^{2}}\,dt=\left[- t - 3 \ln{\left(3 - t \right)} + 3 \ln{\left(t + 3 \right)}\right]_{-1}^{2}=-3 + 3 \ln{\left(2 \right)} + 3 \ln{\left(5 \right)}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The sign of 9−x² determines the correct square root.

(b)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

marking_criteria.description_html: Simplify the speed and choose the correct sign.

questions.title: A spiral crossing its axis of revolution
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=e^{t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad y=e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad - \frac{\pi}{4}\le t\le \frac{\pi}{4}.\]

  1. Find the exact length of the specified arc.

    [5]

  2. Find the exact curved surface area generated by rotation about the \(x\)-axis. Explain why an unsplit signed integral would be wrong.

    [9]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[- \frac{\sqrt{5}}{e^{\frac{\pi}{4}}} + \sqrt{5} e^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\]

(b)

\[\frac{\sqrt{5} \pi \left(-1 + 2 e^{\frac{\pi}{2}} + e^{\pi}\right)}{2 e^{\frac{\pi}{2}}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=- 2 e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + e^{t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 e^{t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=5 e^{2 t}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{- \frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sqrt{5} e^{t}\,dt=\left[\sqrt{5} e^{t}\right]_{- \frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}=- \frac{\sqrt{5}}{e^{\frac{\pi}{4}}} + \sqrt{5} e^{\frac{\pi}{4}}.\]

(b)

The radius is \(|y|=e^t|\sin2t|\). It is negative before the crossing only as a signed coordinate; distance itself is positive. Therefore

\[S=2\pi\sqrt5\left(-\int_{-\pi/4}^0e^{2t}\sin2t\,dt+\int_0^{\pi/4}e^{2t}\sin2t\,dt\right).\]

Two integrations by parts give

\[\int e^{2t}\sin2t\,dt=\frac14e^{2t}(\sin2t-\cos2t).\]

Evaluating each part separately gives

\[S=\frac{\sqrt{5} \pi \left(-1 + 2 e^{\frac{\pi}{2}} + e^{\pi}\right)}{2 e^{\frac{\pi}{2}}}.\]

Using y rather than |y| would subtract the surface below the axis. The parameter does not retrace the arc because its distance from the origin is strictly increasing.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(b)

Split at t=0 and use distance to the axis.

questions.title: An exact secant arc and surface
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(y=4\sec(x/2)\) on \(0\le x\le\pi/3\).

  1. Show that \(ds/dx=2\sec^2(x/2)-1\).

    [4]

  2. Find the exact arc length.

    [3]

  3. Show that \(\frac d{du}(\sec u\tan u)=2\sec^3u-\sec u\), and hence find the surface area about the \(x\)-axis.

    [4]

  4. Find the mean value of \(y\) over the specified \(x\)-interval.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{ds}{dx}=2\sec^2(x/2)-1\]

(b)

\[- \frac{\pi}{3} + \frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\]

(c)

\[\frac{32 \pi}{3}\]

(d)

\[\frac{12 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{\pi}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Here \(y^{\prime}=2\sec(x/2)\tan(x/2)\). Hence

\[1+(y^{\prime})^2=1+4\sec^2(x/2)(\sec^2(x/2)-1)=(2\sec^2(x/2)-1)^2.\]

The expression inside the final square is at least 1, so it is the positive speed.

(b)

\[L=[4\tan(x/2)-x]_0^{\pi/3}=\frac4{\sqrt3}-\frac\pi3.\]

(c)

\[\frac d{du}(\sec u\tan u)=\sec u\tan^2u+\sec^3u=2\sec^3u-\sec u.\]

With \(u=x/2\),

\[S=16\pi\int_0^{\pi/6}(2\sec^3u-\sec u)\,du=16\pi[\sec u\tan u]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac{32\pi}3.\]

(d)

\[\bar y=\frac3\pi\int_0^{\pi/3}4\sec(x/2)\,dx=\frac{24}\pi[\ln(\sec u+\tan u)]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac{12\ln3}\pi.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use tan²=sec²−1.

(b)

Integrate the speed, remembering the factor from x/2.

(c)

Use the displayed derivative to avoid a separate sec³ integral.

(d)

The mean uses the x-interval length.

questions.title: A power arc, enclosed area and volume
questions.prompt_html:

\[x=\frac{5 t^{2}}{2},\qquad y=\frac{5 t^{3}}{3},\qquad 0\le t\le 3.\]

questions.title: A cubic arch: surface and mean ordinate
questions.prompt_html:
The curve is defined parametrically by

\[x=3 t^{2},\qquad y=- t^{3} + 3 t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.\]

  1. Find the exact area of the curved surface generated by rotating this arc through one complete revolution about the \(x\)-axis. Do not include end discs.

    [7]

  2. Find the mean value of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) over the corresponding \(x\)-interval.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{1}\left(- t^{3} + 3 t\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=6 t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=3 - 3 t^{2},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=3 t^{2} + 3.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(- 3 t^{5} + 6 t^{3} + 9 t\right)\,dt=\frac{t^{2} \left(- t^{4} + 3 t^{2} + 9\right)}{2}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{t^{2} \left(- t^{4} + 3 t^{2} + 9\right)}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}=11 \pi.\]

(b)

The \(x\)-coordinate increases over this interval. Its total change is \(3\). Thus

\[\bar y=\frac1{3}\int_{0}^{1}6 t \left(- t^{3} + 3 t\right)\,dt=\frac1{3}\left[\frac{6 t^{3} \left(5 - t^{2}\right)}{5}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac{8}{5}.\]

questions.title: A complete cubic arch and its solid
questions.prompt_html:

  2. Find the volume generated by rotating the region under the arc about the \(x\)-axis.

(a)

The radius y=t(3−t²)/6 is nonnegative throughout this interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\left(- \frac{t^{3}}{6} + \frac{t}{2}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=t,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{1}{2} - \frac{t^{2}}{2},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(- \frac{t^{5}}{12} + \frac{t^{3}}{6} + \frac{t}{4}\right)\,dt=\frac{t^{2} \left(- t^{4} + 3 t^{2} + 9\right)}{72}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{t^{2} \left(- t^{4} + 3 t^{2} + 9\right)}{72}\right]_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{3 \pi}{4}.\]

(b)

\[V=\pi\int_0^{\sqrt3}\frac{t^2(3-t^2)^2}{36}\,t\,dt.\]

Putting \(u=t^2\) gives

\[V=\frac\pi{72}\int_0^3u(3-u)^2\,du=\frac\pi{72}\left[\frac92u^2-2u^3+\frac14u^4\right]_0^3=\frac{3\pi}{32}.\]

questions.title: A secant mean and a logarithmic arc
questions.prompt_html:

Divide the integral by \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) to obtain the mean:

questions.title: A recurrence hidden inside an arc-length problem
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(I_n=\int_0^{\pi/4}t^n\sin(2t)\,dt\). A curve is specified by

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=t^3(1-\cos4t),\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=t^3\sin4t,\qquad0\le t\le\pi/4.\]

\[I_n=\frac n2\int_0^{\pi/4}t^{n-1}\cos2t\,dt=\frac n4(\pi/4)^{n-1}-\frac{n(n-1)}4I_{n-2}.\]

The cosine boundary vanishes in the first integration, and the upper sine value in the second is 1.

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=t^6[(1-\cos4t)^2+\sin^24t]=4t^6\sin^22t.\]

\[4I_3=3(\pi/4)^2-6I_1,\qquad L=2I_3=- \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3 \pi^{2}}{32}.\]

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=2 t \cos{\left(t \right)},\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=2 t \sin{\left(t \right)},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=2 t.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(- 4 t^{2} \cos{\left(t \right)} + 4 t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\,dt=- 4 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} - 12 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 12 \sin{\left(t \right)}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[- 4 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} - 12 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 12 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}=- 4 \pi^{2} - \frac{4 \sqrt{3} \pi^{3}}{9} + 12 \sqrt{3} \pi.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: A logarithmic arc and a square-root surface
questions.prompt_html:
1. Find the exact length of the specified arc. The arc has equation \(y=-3\ln(\cos(x/3))\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\).

    [4]

  2. The curve \(y=3\sqrt{x+1}\) for \(0\le x\le3\) is rotated once about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact curved surface area.

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

Differentiate the coordinates:

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{\sin{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}}{\cos{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}}.\]

Their squared sum simplifies to

\[\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)^2=\sec^{2}{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}.\]

The chosen square root is nonnegative on the stated interval, so

\[L=\int_{0}^{\pi}\sec{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)}\,dt=\left[3 \ln{\left(\tan{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)} + \sec{\left(\frac{t}{3} \right)} \right)}\right]_{0}^{\pi}=3 \ln{\left(\sqrt{3} + 2 \right)}.\]

(b)

For this Cartesian curve take t=x as the parameter.

The radius is nonnegative on the given interval. The surface formula uses distance from the axis, not the other coordinate:

\[S=2\pi\int_{0}^{3}\left(3 \sqrt{t + 1}\right)\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt.\]

Differentiating the coordinates gives

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1,\qquad\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{t + 1}},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\sqrt{1 + \frac{9}{4 \left(t + 1\right)}}.\]

The nonnegative speed is obtained from the sum of the two squared derivatives. The remaining antiderivative is

\[\int \left(3 \sqrt{1 + \frac{9}{4 t + 4}} \sqrt{t + 1}\right)\,dt=\frac{\left(4 t + 13\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{4}+C.\]
\[S=2\pi\left[\frac{\left(4 t + 13\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{4}\right]_{0}^{3}=- \frac{13 \sqrt{13} \pi}{2} + \frac{125 \pi}{2}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify the squared speed first, then choose the nonnegative square root.

(b)

Use the distance to the named axis as radius; include the speed and the factor 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Simplify the speed and choose the correct sign.
Choose the correct radius and surface formula.

questions.title: A rational Riemann sum and its exact limit
questions.prompt_html:
Let N be a positive integer.

Let \(R_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac{N}{N^2+4r^2}\). Use rectangles of width \(1/N\) for \(f(x)=1/(1+4x^2)\) on \([0,1]\).

  1. Show that \(R_N\lt \tfrac12\tan^{-1}2\).

    [4]

  2. Find a strict lower bound for \(R_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]

  3. Deduce \(\lim_{N\to\infty}R_N\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function decreases strictly from 1 to 1/5. Its right-endpoint rectangle sum is

\[\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^N f(r/N)=\sum_{r=1}^N\frac{N}{N^2+4r^2}=R_N.\]

Every right rectangle is below the curve, and

\[\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+4x^2}=\left[\frac12\tan^{-1}(2x)\right]_0^1=\frac12\tan^{-1}2.\]

(b)

The left-endpoint sum exceeds the right-endpoint sum by

\[\frac{f(0)-f(1)}N=\frac4{5N}.\]

The integral is smaller than the left sum, so \(I\lt R_N+4/(5N)\). Rearranging gives the bound.

(c)

The lower and upper bounds both approach \(\frac{\tan^{-1}{\left(2 \right)}}{2}\). The squeeze argument gives the same limit for \(R_N\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Recognise the factor 1/N and the right endpoints.

(b)

The two sums differ only by their first and last heights.

(c)

Use both bounds.

marking_criteria.description_html: Show the bounds have a common limit.

questions.title: An increasing exponential sum
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(N\ge2\), let \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^N e^{2\sqrt r}/\sqrt r\).

  1. Show that \(f(x)=e^{2\sqrt x}/\sqrt x\) is increasing for \(x\ge1\), and find \(\int_1^Nf(x)\,dx\).

    [3]

  2. Use unit-width rectangles to prove

    \[e^{2\sqrt N}\lt S_N\lt \left(1+\frac1{\sqrt N}\right)e^{2\sqrt N}-e^2.\]
    [4]

  3. Deduce \(\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N/e^{2\sqrt N}\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\int_1^Nf(x)\,dx=e^{2\sqrt N}-e^2\]

(b)

\[e^{2\sqrt N}\lt S_N\lt \left(1+\frac1{\sqrt N}\right)e^{2\sqrt N}-e^2\]

(c)

\[1\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{e^{2\sqrt x}(2\sqrt x-1)}{2x^{3/2}}\gt 0\quad(x\ge1).\]

Use \(u=2\sqrt x\) to obtain the stated integral.

(b)

For an increasing function,

\[\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}f(r)\lt \int_1^Nf(x)\,dx\lt \sum_{r=2}^{N}f(r).\]

The left sum is \(S_N-f(N)\) and the right sum is \(S_N-f(1)\). Rearranging each side, then substituting \(f(1)=e^2\), proves the two bounds.

(c)

Divide the bounds by \(e^{2\sqrt N}\). They become \(1\lt S_N/e^{2\sqrt N}\lt 1+N^{-1/2}-e^{2-2\sqrt N}\). Both bounding expressions tend to 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate before choosing upper and lower rectangles.

(b)

Keep track of the single omitted endpoint in each sum.

(c)

Normalise the bounds before taking the limit.

questions.title: Bounds for a reciprocal-cube series
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^Nr^{-3}\), where \(N\ge3\). Use the curve \(y=x^{-3}\) on \(2\le x\le N\).

  1. Use unit-width rectangles to prove \(S_N\gt \frac{9}{8} - \frac{1}{2 N^{2}} + \frac{1}{N^{3}}\).

    [4]

  2. Find a strict upper bound for \(S_N\).

    [4]

  3. Explain why the infinite series converges and give bounds for its sum. Non-strict bounds are sufficient.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[S_N\gt \frac{9}{8} - \frac{1}{2 N^{2}} + \frac{1}{N^{3}}\]

(b)

\[S_N\lt \frac{5}{4} - \frac{1}{2 N^{2}}\]

(c)

\[\frac98\le\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac1{r^3}\le\frac54\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function is positive and decreasing. Left-endpoint rectangles give

\[\int_2^Nx^{-3}\,dx\lt \sum_{r=2}^{N-1}r^{-3}=S_N-1-N^{-3}.\]
\[\int_2^Nx^{-3}\,dx=\frac18-\frac1{2N^2}.\]

Rearrange to obtain the required lower bound.

(b)

Right-endpoint rectangles give

\[S_N-1-\frac18=\sum_{r=3}^{N}r^{-3}\lt \int_2^Nx^{-3}\,dx=\frac18-\frac1{2N^2}.\]

Thus \(S_N\lt \frac{5}{4} - \frac{1}{2 N^{2}}\).

(c)

The partial sums increase because all terms are positive, and they are bounded above by 5/4. They therefore converge. Taking limits in the inequalities gives the displayed non-strict bounds.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

For the lower bound on the sum, use an upper rectangle estimate for the integral.

(b)

Restore both r=1 and r=2.

(c)

A strict inequality for each finite N need not remain strict after taking limits.

questions.title: An increasing quadratic and exact rectangle sums
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=- x^{2} + 3 x.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Find an exact formula for \(U_N\) and justify why it is a strict upper bound for the integral.

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]

  3. Show that \(U_N-L_N\to0\) and deduce the limit of both sums.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac{\left(N + 1\right) \left(7 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac{\left(N - 1\right) \left(7 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]

(c)

\[\lim L_N=\lim U_N=\frac{7}{6}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function is strictly increasing on the interval. Thus left endpoints give the lower rectangles and right endpoints give the upper rectangles. Each endpoint rectangle has a positive area discrepancy from the curved strip, so \(L_N\lt \int_0^1f(x)\,dx\lt U_N\).

\[U_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(\frac{3 r}{N} - \frac{r^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).\]

Expand the summand and apply the standard sums of the relevant powers of r:

\[U_N=\frac{\left(N + 1\right) \left(7 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}.\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\left(\frac{3 r}{N} - \frac{r^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).\]

Use the same power sums, or subtract the endpoint difference from the upper sum:

\[L_N=\frac{\left(N - 1\right) \left(7 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}},\qquad U_N-L_N=\frac{2}{N}.\]

(c)

\[U_N-L_N=\frac{2}{N}\longrightarrow0.\]

Both exact expressions also tend to \(\frac{7}{6}\), which agrees with \(\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the endpoint at which the function is largest on each subinterval.

(b)

The difference of the endpoint sums telescopes.

(c)

Use the endpoint difference before taking limits.

marking_criteria.description_html: Evaluate or subtract the telescoping endpoint difference.

questions.title: A decreasing translated quadratic
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=\left(2 - x\right)^{2}.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Find an exact formula for \(U_N\) and justify why it is a strict upper bound for the integral.

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]

  3. Show that \(U_N-L_N\to0\) and deduce the limit of both sums.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac{\left(2 N + 1\right) \left(7 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac{\left(2 N - 1\right) \left(7 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]

(c)

\[\lim L_N=\lim U_N=\frac{7}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function is strictly decreasing on the interval. Thus right endpoints give the lower rectangles and left endpoints give the upper rectangles. Each endpoint rectangle has a positive area discrepancy from the curved strip, so \(L_N\lt \int_0^1f(x)\,dx\lt U_N\).

\[U_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\left(\left(2 - \frac{r}{N}\right)^{2}\right).\]

Expand the summand and apply the standard sums of the relevant powers of r:

\[U_N=\frac{\left(2 N + 1\right) \left(7 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}.\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(\left(2 - \frac{r}{N}\right)^{2}\right).\]

Use the same power sums, or subtract the endpoint difference from the upper sum:

\[L_N=\frac{\left(2 N - 1\right) \left(7 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}},\qquad U_N-L_N=\frac{3}{N}.\]

(c)

\[U_N-L_N=\frac{3}{N}\longrightarrow0.\]

Both exact expressions also tend to \(\frac{7}{3}\), which agrees with \(\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the endpoint at which the function is largest on each subinterval.

(b)

The difference of the endpoint sums telescopes.

(c)

Use the endpoint difference before taking limits.

marking_criteria.description_html: Evaluate or subtract the telescoping endpoint difference.

questions.title: Inverse hyperbolic sums bounded by integration
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(N\ge1\), define \(T_N=\sum_{r=1}^N\sinh^{-1}(r/2)\).

  1. Find \(\int\sinh^{-1}(x/2)\,dx\).

    [3]

  2. Show that \(T_N\gt N \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} - \sqrt{N^{2} + 4} + 2\).

    [4]

  3. Find a strict upper bound for \(T_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[C + x \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} \right)} - \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\]

(b)

\[T_N\gt N \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} - \sqrt{N^{2} + 4} + 2\]

(c)

\[T_N\lt N \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} - \sqrt{N^{2} + 4} + \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} + 2\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate by parts with \(u=\sinh^{-1}(x/2)\) and \(dv=dx\). Since \(du=dx/\sqrt{x^2+4}\),

\[\int\sinh^{-1}(x/2)\,dx=x\sinh^{-1}(x/2)-\int\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\,dx=x\sinh^{-1}(x/2)-\sqrt{x^2+4}+C.\]

(b)

The function is strictly increasing on \(x\ge0\). Right-endpoint rectangles of width 1 on \([0,N]\) have total area \(T_N\) and lie above the curve. Hence

\[T_N\gt \int_0^N\sinh^{-1}(x/2)\,dx=N \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} - \sqrt{N^{2} + 4} + 2.\]

(c)

The left-endpoint sum on the same intervals is \(T_N-\sinh^{-1}(N/2)\) because the height at zero is zero. It is smaller than the integral, so

\[T_N\lt \int_0^Nf(x)\,dx+f(N)=N \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} - \sqrt{N^{2} + 4} + \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{N}{2} \right)} + 2.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate the remaining x/√(x²+4) by substitution.

(b)

Here the first interval is [0,1], not [1,2].

(c)

The two rectangle sums differ by f(N)−f(0).

questions.title: Exponential rectangles and a limiting expansion
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=e^{2 - 2 x}.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Show that \(U_N=\frac{-1 + e^{2}}{N \left(1 - e^{- \frac{2}{N}}\right)}\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) and justify the two strict comparisons with the integral.

    [4]

  3. Simplify \(U_N-L_N\) and find its limit.

    [3]

  4. Find the first three terms of \(z(1-e^{-2/z})\) in ascending powers of \(1/z\). Hence determine \(\lim_{N\to\infty}U_N\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac{-1 + e^{2}}{N \left(1 - e^{- \frac{2}{N}}\right)}\]

(b)

\[L_N=e^{-2/N}U_N\]

(c)

\[U_N-L_N=\frac{e^2-1}N\to0\]

(d)

\[z(1-e^{-2/z})=2-\frac2z+\frac4{3z^2}+O(z^{-3}),\qquad\lim U_N=\frac{e^2-1}2\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the left endpoints because the function decreases:

\[U_N=\frac{e^2}N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}(e^{-2/N})^r=\frac{e^2(1-e^{-2})}{N(1-e^{-2/N})}.\]

Simplifying the numerator gives the required form.

(b)

The right endpoint of each subinterval is 1/N to the right of the left endpoint, so every height is multiplied by \(e^{-2/N}\). Thus \(L_N=e^{-2/N}U_N\). Strict decrease gives \(L_N\lt \int_0^1f(x)\,dx\lt U_N\).

(c)

\[U_N-L_N=(1-e^{-2/N})U_N=\frac{e^2-1}N\longrightarrow0.\]

(d)

Use \(e^w=1+w+w^2/2+w^3/6+O(w^4)\) with \(w=-2/z\):

\[e^{-2/z}=1-\frac2z+\frac2{z^2}-\frac4{3z^3}+O(z^{-4}).\]

Subtract from 1 and multiply by z. In particular the denominator of U_N tends to 2, giving the stated limit.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Sum a geometric progression with N terms.

(b)

Relate corresponding heights instead of summing again.

(c)

Cancel the factor before taking the limit.

(d)

Expand one order further before multiplying by z.

questions.title: Rectangle accuracy and bounds for a logarithm
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=3^{- x}.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Show that \(L_N=\frac2{3N(3^{1/N}-1)}\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(U_N\) and simplify \(U_N-L_N\).

    [3]

  3. Find the least \(N\) for which \(U_N-L_N\le1/2000\).

    [3]

  4. Use this value of \(N\) to give exact upper and lower bounds for \(\ln3\). You may leave powers of 3 unevaluated.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[L_N=\frac{2}{3 N \left(3^{\frac{1}{N}} - 1\right)}\]

(b)

\[U_N=3^{1/N}L_N,\qquad U_N-L_N=\frac2{3N}\]

(c)

\[N=1334\]

(d)

\[1334(1-3^{-1/1334})\lt \ln3\lt 1334(3^{1/1334}-1)\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The lower rectangles use right endpoints. Sum the geometric progression:

\[L_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^N3^{-r/N}=\frac{3^{-1/N}(1-1/3)}{N(1-3^{-1/N})}=\frac2{3N(3^{1/N}-1)}.\]

(b)

The left heights are \(3^{1/N}\) times the right heights. Consequently

\[U_N-L_N=(3^{1/N}-1)L_N=\frac2{3N}.\]

(c)

\[\frac2{3N}\le\frac1{2000}\iff N\ge\frac{4000}3.\]

The least integer is 1334; 1333 does not satisfy the condition.

(d)

The integral equals \(2/(3\ln3)\). Since \(L_N\lt I\lt U_N\) and all quantities are positive, taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities:

\[\frac2{3U_N}\lt \ln3\lt \frac2{3L_N}.\]

Substitute N=1334 and the exact expressions for L_N and U_N to obtain the bounds. Leaving them exact avoids inward rounding.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Multiply numerator and denominator by 3^(1/N).

(b)

Use the ratio of adjacent rectangle heights.

(c)

Round the lower bound upwards.

(d)

Reverse the inequalities when taking reciprocals.

questions.title: Choose the decreasing part before comparing a sum
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=x\operatorname{sech}^2(2x)\) for \(x\ge0\).

  1. Show that the positive stationary point satisfies \(4x\tanh(2x)=1\), and verify that it lies between 0.3 and 0.4. Explain why f decreases for \(x\ge1\).

    [4]

  2. For integers \(N\ge2\), prove

    \[\sum_{r=2}^N r\operatorname{sech}^2(2r)\lt F(N)-F(1),\qquad F(x)=\frac x2\tanh2x-\frac14\ln\cosh2x.\]
    [4]

  3. Deduce an upper bound for \(\sum_{r=2}^{\infty}r\operatorname{sech}^2(2r)\). A non-strict bound is sufficient.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[0.3\lt \alpha\lt 0.4\]

(b)

\[\sum_{r=2}^N r\operatorname{sech}^2(2r)\lt F(N)-F(1)\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=2}^{\infty}r\operatorname{sech}^2(2r)\le\frac14\ln2-\frac12\tanh2+\frac14\ln\cosh2\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\operatorname{sech}^2(2x)[1-4x\tanh(2x)].\]

The function \(g(x)=4x\tanh(2x)\) is strictly increasing for x>0, since \(g^{\prime}(x)=4\tanh(2x)+8x\operatorname{sech}^2(2x)\gt 0\). Its values at 0.3 and 0.4 are approximately 0.6445 and 1.0625. Hence there is a unique stationary point in that interval, and the derivative is negative for x≥1.

(b)

Use right-endpoint unit rectangles on [1,N], where f is strictly decreasing. They lie below the curve. Integration by parts gives

\[\int x\operatorname{sech}^2(2x)\,dx=\frac x2\tanh2x-\frac12\int\tanh2x\,dx=F(x).\]

The rectangle comparison now proves the bound.

(c)

Using \(\ln\cosh2x=2x-\ln2+\ln(1+e^{-4x})\) and \(\tanh2x=(1-e^{-4x})/(1+e^{-4x})\) gives \(F(x)\to\ln2/4\). The partial sums are positive, increasing and bounded; taking limits yields the stated upper bound.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Establish uniqueness using the monotonicity of 4x tanh(2x).

(b)

Do not use an interval across the maximum without checking monotonicity.

(c)

Keep the cancellation of the two linear-in-x terms.

questions.title: An exponential sum with a strict accuracy threshold
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=4^{x}.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Obtain an exact expression for \(U_N\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) and \(U_N-L_N\).

    [3]

  3. Find the least integer \(N\) such that \(U_N-L_N\lt 10^{-4}\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The increasing curve uses right endpoints for the upper sum:

\[U_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^N4^{r/N}=\frac{3\,4^{1/N}}{N(4^{1/N}-1)}.\]

(b)

Shift the index to include r=0 and omit r=N. The difference of the sums is \([f(1)-f(0)]/N=3/N\). This gives the stated lower sum.

(c)

\[3/N\lt 10^{-4}\iff N\gt 30000.\]

At N=30000 the gap equals, rather than is less than, the tolerance. Hence the least permissible value is 30001.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the geometric sum with ratio 4^(1/N).

(b)

The endpoint gap is simpler than either sum.

(c)

Check equality at the integer boundary.

questions.title: Logarithmic rectangles and factorial ratios
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=\ln{\left(x + 2 \right)}.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Show that \(U_N=\frac1N\ln\frac{(3N)!}{(2N)!}-\ln N\).

    [4]

  2. Find a similar exact expression for \(L_N\).

    [3]

  3. Find \(U_N-L_N\) and deduce the limit of both sums.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac1N\ln\frac{(3N)!}{(2N)!}-\ln N\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac1N\ln\frac{(3N-1)!}{(2N-1)!}-\ln N\]

(c)

\[U_N-L_N=\frac{\ln(3/2)}N,\qquad\lim L_N=\lim U_N=3\ln3-2\ln2-1\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The right-endpoint sum is \(N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N\ln((2N+r)/N)\). Add the logarithms by multiplying their arguments: the numerator is the product from 2N+1 to 3N, namely \((3N)!/(2N)!\). The denominator is \(N^N\), which contributes \(-\ln N\) after division by N.

(b)

The left-endpoint numerator now runs from 2N to 3N−1. Its product is \((3N-1)!/(2N-1)!\). The denominator remains Nᴺ.

(c)

All interior terms cancel, giving \((f(1)-f(0))/N=\ln(3/2)/N\to0\). The integral lies between the two sums, and

\[\int_0^1\ln(2+x)\,dx=[(2+x)\ln(2+x)-(2+x)]_0^1=3\ln3-2\ln2-1.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Turn the sum of logarithms into a product.

(b)

Change both ends of the product.

(c)

Evaluate the integral rather than using a factorial asymptotic formula.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the two-sided bound for the limit.

questions.title: A hyperbolic graph and a strict infinite-sum bound
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(f(x)=\operatorname{sech}(2x)\) for real \(x\).

In parts (d) and (e), N is a positive integer.

  1. Starting from exponential definitions, prove \(1+\sinh^2u=\cosh^2u\).

    [3]

  2. Show that \(\frac d{dx}[\tfrac12\tan^{-1}(\sinh2x)]=\operatorname{sech}2x\).

    [2]

  3. Sketch the graph, stating its maximum and horizontal asymptote.

    [2]

  4. Prove that \(\sum_{r=1}^N\operatorname{sech}(2r)\lt \tfrac12\tan^{-1}(\sinh2N)\).

    [3]

  5. Prove that the corresponding infinite sum is strictly less than \(\pi/4\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[1+\sinh^2u=\cosh^2u\]

(b)

\[F^{\prime}(x)=\operatorname{sech}2x\]

(c)

Even, with maximum \((0,1)\) and asymptote \(y=0\).

(d)

\[\sum_{r=1}^N\operatorname{sech}(2r)\lt \frac12\tan^{-1}(\sinh2N)\]

(e)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{sech}(2r)\lt \frac\pi4\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\cosh^2u-\sinh^2u=\frac{(e^u+e^{-u})^2-(e^u-e^{-u})^2}{4}=1.\]

(b)

\[F^{\prime}(x)=\frac12\frac{2\cosh2x}{1+\sinh^22x}=\frac1{\cosh2x}.\]

(c)

The function is positive and even; cosh(2x)≥1 gives the maximum at zero. As |x| grows, cosh(2x) grows without bound, so the ordinate approaches zero. It decreases strictly for x>0.

(d)

Right-endpoint unit rectangles on [0,N] lie strictly below the decreasing curve. Their total area is the sum. Integrating the curve using part (b) gives the right-hand side, since F(0)=0.

(e)

The first rectangle leaves a fixed positive gap \(\delta=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx-f(1)\gt 0\). Thus for every N, \(\sum_{r=1}^Nf(r)\le\int_0^Nf(x)\,dx-\delta\). The partial sums are increasing and bounded; their limit is at most \(\pi/4-\delta\lt \pi/4\). This fixed gap justifies retaining strictness after taking the limit.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the difference of squares.

(b)

Use the preceding identity after applying the chain rule.

(c)

Use reciprocal cosh and symmetry.

(d)

The lower limit of the comparison integral is zero.

(e)

Use the positive gap on the first interval.

marking_criteria.description_html: Pass to the limit and retain a strict bound.

questions.title: A root denominator and two-sided sum bounds
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(N\ge2\), define \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^N\frac1{\sqrt{r^2+4r}}\).

  1. Find an antiderivative of \(f(x)=1/\sqrt{x^2+4x}\) for \(x\gt 0\).

    [3]

  2. Use unit rectangles to obtain a strict upper bound for \(S_N\). Give it in logarithmic form.

    [4]

  3. Find a strict lower bound using the same comparison interval.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[C + \cosh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} + 1 \right)}\]

(b)

\[S_N\lt \ln\frac{N+2+\sqrt{N^2+4N}}{3+\sqrt5}+\frac1{\sqrt5}\]

(c)

\[S_N\gt \ln\frac{N+2+\sqrt{N^2+4N}}{3+\sqrt5}+\frac1{\sqrt{N^2+4N}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Complete the square \(x^2+4x=(x+2)^2-4\). The standard inverse hyperbolic form gives \(\cosh^{-1}((x+2)/2)+C\). Its logarithmic form is \(\ln((x+2+\sqrt{x^2+4x})/2)+C\).

(b)

The positive function decreases on [1,N]. Therefore \(S_N-f(1)\lt \int_1^Nf(x)\,dx\). The integral is

\[\ln\frac{N+2+\sqrt{N^2+4N}}{3+\sqrt5}.\]

Add \(f(1)=1/\sqrt5\) to obtain the upper bound.

(c)

Left rectangles give \(\int_1^N f(x)\,dx\lt S_N-f(N)\). Add the final term and use the same integral.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Complete the square before choosing the inverse function.

(b)

Use right rectangles on [1,N] and restore the first term.

(c)

The missing term is now the last term.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply the inverse hyperbolic formula with its scale.

questions.title: A cubic-linear rectangle sum with an accuracy target
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=x^{3} + x.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Find an exact formula for \(U_N\) and justify why it is a strict upper bound for the integral.

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [3]

  3. Find the least integer \(N\) such that \(U_N-L_N\lt \frac{1}{1000}\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac{\left(N + 1\right) \left(3 N + 1\right)}{4 N^{2}}\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac{\left(N - 1\right) \left(3 N - 1\right)}{4 N^{2}}\]

(c)

\[N=2001\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function is strictly increasing on the interval. Thus left endpoints give the lower rectangles and right endpoints give the upper rectangles. Each endpoint rectangle has a positive area discrepancy from the curved strip, so \(L_N\lt \int_0^1f(x)\,dx\lt U_N\).

\[U_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(\frac{r}{N} + \frac{r^{3}}{N^{3}}\right).\]

Expand the summand and apply the standard sums of the relevant powers of r:

\[U_N=\frac{\left(N + 1\right) \left(3 N + 1\right)}{4 N^{2}}.\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\left(\frac{r}{N} + \frac{r^{3}}{N^{3}}\right).\]

Use the same power sums, or subtract the endpoint difference from the upper sum:

\[L_N=\frac{\left(N - 1\right) \left(3 N - 1\right)}{4 N^{2}},\qquad U_N-L_N=\frac{2}{N}.\]

(c)

\[\frac{2}{N}\lt \frac{1}{1000}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N\gt 2000.\]

The least admissible integer is \(2001\). At the previous integer the condition fails.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the endpoint at which the function is largest on each subinterval.

(b)

The difference of the endpoint sums telescopes.

(c)

Distinguish a strict bound from a non-strict one.

marking_criteria.description_html: Evaluate or subtract the telescoping endpoint difference.

questions.title: A logarithmic reciprocal series
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(N\ge3\), let \(T_N=\sum_{r=2}^N(\ln r)/r^3\).

  1. Show that \(f(x)=(\ln x)/x^3\) decreases for \(x\ge2\) and find its antiderivative.

    [3]

  2. Obtain strict lower and upper bounds for \(T_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]

  3. Deduce convergence and give non-strict bounds for \(\sum_{r=2}^{\infty}(\ln r)/r^3\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[C + \frac{- 2 \ln{\left(x \right)} - 1}{4 x^{2}}\]

(b)

\[J_N+\frac{\ln N}{N^3}\lt T_N\lt J_N+\frac{\ln2}{8},\qquad J_N=\frac{1}{16} + \frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{8} + \frac{- 2 \ln{\left(N \right)} - 1}{4 N^{2}}\]

(c)

\[\frac{2\ln2+1}{16}\le\sum_{r=2}^{\infty}\frac{\ln r}{r^3}\le\frac{4\ln2+1}{16}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1-3\ln x}{x^4}\lt 0\quad(x\ge2).\]

Integration by parts gives

\[\int\frac{\ln x}{x^3}\,dx=-\frac{\ln x}{2x^2}-\frac1{4x^2}+C.\]

(b)

On [2,N], right and left unit rectangles give

\[T_N-f(2)\lt \int_2^Nf(x)\,dx\lt T_N-f(N).\]

The integral is J_N as displayed. Rearranging gives both bounds.

(c)

The partial sums are positive and increasing, and the upper bound is bounded. Also \((\ln N)/N^2\to0\) and \((\ln N)/N^3\to0\). Taking limits gives the displayed bounds.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use integration by parts with u=ln x.

(b)

Match the first retained summand r=2.

(c)

Do not claim that a finite strict inequality automatically has a strict limit.

questions.title: Rectangle bounds for a quadratic with a linear term
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=x^{2} + 2 x.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Find an exact formula for \(U_N\) and justify why it is a strict upper bound for the integral.

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac{\left(N + 1\right) \left(8 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac{\left(N - 1\right) \left(8 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function is strictly increasing on the interval. Thus left endpoints give the lower rectangles and right endpoints give the upper rectangles. Each endpoint rectangle has a positive area discrepancy from the curved strip, so \(L_N\lt \int_0^1f(x)\,dx\lt U_N\).

\[U_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(\frac{2 r}{N} + \frac{r^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).\]

Expand the summand and apply the standard sums of the relevant powers of r:

\[U_N=\frac{\left(N + 1\right) \left(8 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}.\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\left(\frac{2 r}{N} + \frac{r^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).\]

Use the same power sums, or subtract the endpoint difference from the upper sum:

\[L_N=\frac{\left(N - 1\right) \left(8 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}},\qquad U_N-L_N=\frac{3}{N}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the endpoint at which the function is largest on each subinterval.

(b)

The difference of the endpoint sums telescopes.

marking_criteria.description_html: Evaluate or subtract the telescoping endpoint difference.

questions.title: Bounding an odd-factor product
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(P_N=\prod_{r=1}^N(2r+1)\) for integers \(N\ge2\).

  1. By considering unit-width rectangles for \(y=\ln(2x+1)\), find a strict lower bound for \(\ln P_N\).

    [4]

  2. Find a strict upper bound for \(\ln P_N\), and express \(P_N\) using factorials.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\ln P_N\gt \frac{(2N+1)\ln(2N+1)-(2N+1)-\ln3+3}{2}\]

(b)

\[\ln P_N\lt \frac{(2N+3)\ln(2N+1)-(2N+1)-3\ln3+3}{2},\qquad P_N=\frac{(2N+1)!}{2^NN!}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The curve is increasing. Right rectangles on [1,N] give

\[\int_1^N\ln(2x+1)\,dx\lt \sum_{r=2}^N\ln(2r+1)=\ln P_N-\ln3.\]

With \(F(x)=((2x+1)\ln(2x+1)-(2x+1))/2\), the integral is F(N)−F(1). Add ln3 and simplify.

(b)

Left rectangles give \(\ln P_N-\ln(2N+1)\lt F(N)-F(1)\). Add the last logarithm to obtain the upper bound. In the factorial \((2N+1)!\), the product of even factors is \(2^NN!\); division leaves exactly the odd factors, including the harmless factor 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Add back the r=1 factor after comparing with the integral.

(b)

The left sum omits the final odd factor.

questions.title: A rational sum with logarithmic growth
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(N\ge2\), let \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^N r/(3r^2-2)\).

  1. Show that \(f(x)=x/(3x^2-2)\) is positive and decreasing for \(x\ge1\), and find \(\int_1^Nf(x)\,dx\).

    [3]

  2. Use unit-width rectangles to prove

    \[\frac16\ln(3N^2-2)+\frac{N}{3N^2-2}\lt S_N\lt \frac16\ln(3N^2-2)+1.\]
    [4]

  3. Deduce whether the infinite series converges, and find \(\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N/\ln N\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\int_1^Nf(x)\,dx=\frac16\ln(3N^2-2)\]

(b)

\[J_N+f(N)\lt S_N\lt J_N+1\]

(c)

\[S_N\to+\infty,\qquad \frac{S_N}{\ln N}\to\frac13\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=-\frac{3x^2+2}{(3x^2-2)^2}\lt 0.\]

The denominator is positive for x≥1. Substitution \(u=3x^2-2\) evaluates the integral; its lower logarithm is ln1=0.

(b)

For a decreasing curve on [1,N],

\[S_N-f(1)\lt \int_1^Nf(x)\,dx\lt S_N-f(N).\]

Here f(1)=1. Substitute the integral and rearrange.

(c)

The lower bound tends to infinity, so the series diverges. Divide both bounds by lnN. The main term satisfies

\[\frac{\ln(3N^2-2)}{6\ln N}=\frac13+\frac{\ln(3-2/N^2)}{6\ln N}\to\frac13.\]

The extra endpoint terms divided by lnN tend to zero. The squeeze argument gives the limit.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The derivative of the denominator is a multiple of the numerator.

(b)

Use both endpoint comparisons on exactly the same interval.

(c)

Separate 2lnN from the logarithm of the quadratic.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the lower bound to prove divergence.

questions.title: A two-sided square-root sum estimate
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(N\ge1\), let \(T_N=\sum_{r=1}^N1/\sqrt{r^2+2r+5}\).

  1. Find \(\int_0^N dx/\sqrt{x^2+2x+5}\) in logarithmic form.

    [3]

  2. Use unit-width rectangles to show that \(T_N\lt J_N\).

    [4]

  3. Find a strict lower bound for \(T_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[J_N=\ln\frac{N+1+\sqrt{N^2+2N+5}}{1+\sqrt5}\]

(b)

\[T_N\lt J_N\]

(c)

\[T_N\gt J_N-\frac1{\sqrt5}+\frac1{\sqrt{N^2+2N+5}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Complete the square \(x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4\). An antiderivative is \(\sinh^{-1}((x+1)/2)\). Converting its endpoint difference to logarithms gives the stated J_N.

(b)

The function \(f(x)=1/\sqrt{x^2+2x+5}\) is positive and strictly decreasing for x≥0, since its derivative is \(-(x+1)(x^2+2x+5)^{-3/2}\lt 0\). Right-endpoint rectangles on [0,N] have total area T_N and lie strictly below the curve.

(c)

The left-endpoint sum is \(T_N+f(0)-f(N)\) and lies above the integral. Rearrange \(J_N\lt T_N+f(0)-f(N)\) using f(0)=1/√5.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the positive plus-square inverse hyperbolic form.

(b)

The comparison starts at x=0 even though the sum starts at r=1.

(c)

Use the exact endpoint difference between the sums.

questions.title: A decreasing quadratic and exact lower and upper sums
questions.prompt_html:
For a positive integer \(N\), divide \([0,1]\) into \(N\) equal subintervals. Let \(L_N\) and \(U_N\) be the lower and upper rectangle sums for

\[f(x)=2 - x^{2}.\]

Each rectangle has width \(1/N\). State which endpoints give the lower and upper heights.

  1. Find an exact formula for \(U_N\) and justify why it is a strict upper bound for the integral.

    [4]

  2. Find \(L_N\) in terms of \(N\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[U_N=\frac{\left(2 N + 1\right) \left(5 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac{\left(2 N - 1\right) \left(5 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function is strictly decreasing on the interval. Thus right endpoints give the lower rectangles and left endpoints give the upper rectangles. Each endpoint rectangle has a positive area discrepancy from the curved strip, so \(L_N\lt \int_0^1f(x)\,dx\lt U_N\).

\[U_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}\left(2 - \frac{r^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).\]

Expand the summand and apply the standard sums of the relevant powers of r:

\[U_N=\frac{\left(2 N + 1\right) \left(5 N - 1\right)}{6 N^{2}}.\]

(b)

\[L_N=\frac1N\sum_{r=1}^{N}\left(2 - \frac{r^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).\]

Use the same power sums, or subtract the endpoint difference from the upper sum:

\[L_N=\frac{\left(2 N - 1\right) \left(5 N + 1\right)}{6 N^{2}},\qquad U_N-L_N=\frac{1}{N}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the endpoint at which the function is largest on each subinterval.

(b)

The difference of the endpoint sums telescopes.

marking_criteria.description_html: Evaluate or subtract the telescoping endpoint difference.
